AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: What AI Refers To
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: AI can refer broadly to programs that follow human-written rules as well as generative systems that learn patterns from data. The key distinctions lie in how these systems work and how the different technologies fit together.
objectives: Distinguish how rule-based programs and machine-learning systems operate.
Explain how artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI fit inside one another.
Identify systems that look similar but work differently under the surface.

steps.title: How two kinds of chatbots work
steps.contentMarkdown:
Chatbots can look alike while working in very different ways.

Open the help window on an online store and buttons usually come first. Track an order. Start a return. Ask about billing. Press one and a message someone wrote in advance appears. Type a question that no button covers, and the window may repeat itself or fail to respond properly.

A recent generative AI chatbot accepts freely written sentences. Faced with a question it has never seen, it composes a new answer on the spot. The response may sound natural, but its content is not always correct.

The first system follows choices and rules set by people. The second creates a new response from patterns learned in data. Both may be called AI, so the label alone is not enough. To understand what a chatbot can do, you have to ask how it processes a request internally.

steps.title: Who sets the rules
steps.contentMarkdown:
Rule-based programs and machine learning differ in **who sets the rules**. Spam filtering shows the distinction clearly.

With **rule-based filtering**, a person writes every condition. Filter a message if its subject contains `free`. Block it if the sender appears on a particular list. Because the conditions are explicit, it is easy to explain why a message was classified as spam. But a sender might type `f r e e` with spaces and slip past the existing condition. Someone then has to add a new rule.

With **machine learning**, the system receives hundreds of thousands of spam messages and hundreds of thousands of legitimate messages as training data. It looks across many features, such as word combinations, the number of links, and the time a message was sent, and finds patterns that separate the two groups.

If a person writes the conditions directly, the system is rule-based. If the system finds the rules in data, it uses machine learning.
steps.imageAlt: A workbench where the same pebbles are sorted by a fixed hole rule on the left and by comparison with three shape examples on the right

steps.title: How AI technologies fit together
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI are not four technologies of equal scope. **Machine learning sits inside AI, deep learning sits inside machine learning, and generative AI sits inside deep learning.**

| Category | Scope | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Artificial intelligence | Any technique that stands in for human judgment | Rule-based diagnostic programs |
| Machine learning | Techniques that find rules in data | Spam classification, demand forecasting |
| Deep learning | Techniques that use neural networks with multiple layers | Face recognition, translation |
| Generative AI | Techniques that produce new output | Chatbots, image generation |

Diagnostic programs used in hospitals in the 1980s were also called artificial intelligence. They contained thousands of conditional statements written by people and did not learn from data. By contrast, AI in today's news usually refers to generative AI.

Treating a feature of AI as a whole as though it belonged specifically to generative AI gets the scope wrong. Applying the characteristics of generative AI to every kind of AI creates the same problem in reverse.

steps.title: Recognition and generation
steps.contentMarkdown:
Deep learning first achieved strong results at **recognizing things**. It could examine a photo and distinguish a cat from a dog, convert handwriting into digits, or turn speech into text. Each task selects from a fixed set of answers, so the result is relatively easy to score. At a 2012 image-recognition competition, a neural network sharply reduced the error rate.

**Producing something new** is harder to judge because there may be no single correct answer. Ask for a drawing of a cat and many different images could satisfy the request. People may also disagree about which result is better.

Generative AI handles creation by reframing it as a problem of predicting what comes next. It predicts the next word or pixel, or predicts what an image should look like after noise is removed. Repeating such predictions countless times produces a sentence or an image.

Recognition systems classify or identify their input. Generative AI uses what it learned to create new output.

steps.title: How to evaluate an AI product
steps.contentMarkdown:
A product description that says AI does not reveal how the product works internally. Even an automation program made from a hundred conditional statements may be given the AI label. A few checks can help clarify what is underneath.

- **Does the result vary for the same input?** If identical input always produces the same result, the system is more likely to be rule-based.
- **Can it handle unfamiliar input?** See whether it stops or repeats the same response after you move beyond a prepared list.
- **Does the provider explain what it learned from?** The training material affects the character of the results.
- **How are errors handled?** Look for a process in which a person reviews an incorrect result.

Explanations of generative AI use concepts such as training and inference, neural networks, tokens, and attention. Understanding these mechanisms helps you decide how much confidence to place in the output and how far you should rely on it.

quiz.question: Where does machine learning part ways with a rule-based program?
choices: It processes input faster
Instead of a person writing the rules, the rules are found in data
It requires an internet connection
Its results are easier to explain
quiz.explanation: In a rule-based system a person writes the conditions by hand. Machine learning receives example data and lets the program work out the rule that separates the categories.

quiz.question: Which statement describes the relationship among artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI?
choices: They are four separate technologies with no overlap
Generative AI is the broadest and artificial intelligence the narrowest
Machine learning sits inside artificial intelligence, deep learning inside machine learning, and generative AI inside deep learning
Deep learning and machine learning mean the same thing
quiz.explanation: The four layers are nested rather than parallel. Artificial intelligence is the outermost circle and generative AI the innermost.

quiz.question: How does generative AI produce output when no single correct answer exists?
choices: It picks the closest match from results prepared in advance
It rewrites the task as predicting what comes next and chains those predictions together
It runs through rules a person laid out, in order
It copies results found on the internet without changing them
quiz.explanation: Generation is hard to score directly. The task gets rewritten as predicting the next word or the next pixel, and those predictions are chained into a finished result.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: How Training Differs from Inference
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Building a generative AI model and using it to produce answers are separate stages. This lesson explains why conversations do not immediately become training data and how knowledge cutoffs and training data limit a model’s answers.
objectives: Explain when and how training differs from inference
Distinguish generalization from overfitting using examples
Assess limitations caused by knowledge cutoffs and training data

steps.title: How training differs from inference
steps.contentMarkdown:
Using generative AI involves two separate stages: **training** and **inference**.

During training, developers run large numbers of computing devices for weeks or months to build a model. When training ends, the numbers inside the model are fixed at particular values.

Inference begins when a user enters a question and receives an answer, usually within seconds. The model does not change its internal numbers during this process. It uses the values set during training to produce the response.

Think of training as compiling a dictionary and inference as looking up a word in the finished book. Opening the dictionary again and again does not rewrite its contents.

Training may take weeks or months. A single inference usually takes only a few seconds.
steps.imageAlt: One metalworking factory with slow steel die making in the rear and repeated stamping from the finished die in front

steps.title: Why conversations do not train the model
steps.contentMarkdown:
Correct a chatbot’s wrong answer, and the correction can guide its responses for the rest of the current conversation. The model itself does not change.

Continue in the same conversation, and it can refer to the earlier correction. Open a new conversation and ask the same question, however, and the original mistake may return. During inference, none of the model’s internal numbers are updated.

Memory features work in much the same way. They store something the user said separately, then provide it as material for the model to read when a later conversation begins. They do not retrain the model.

User conversations may sometimes be collected for a later round of training. Their contents might influence a new model built months afterward, but they are not learned immediately during the conversation.

steps.title: Generalization and overfitting
steps.contentMarkdown:
Developers train models to handle inputs they have never seen before. This ability is called **generalization**. Getting only the training material right is not enough.

Picture a student who memorized a hundred past exams along with their answer keys. Give the student one of those exams again, and the score may be perfect. Present a new problem, and the student may be unable to solve it. The student memorized where the answers appeared without learning the method. This is **overfitting**.

To detect it, developers divide the available material. Most is used for training, while some is held back for testing. If performance on the training material keeps improving while performance on the held-back material begins to fall, the model may be memorizing the data instead of learning its patterns.

The opposite problem also occurs. If the model’s structure is too simple, it cannot find the patterns at all. It then performs poorly on both the training material and unfamiliar material.

steps.title: Knowledge cutoffs and current information
steps.contentMarkdown:
Developers train a model on material collected up to a particular point. The date when that collection ends is the model’s **knowledge cutoff**.

Events after the cutoff are absent from the training material. Asked about them, a model may admit that it does not know or invent an answer that sounds factual. Information from close to the cutoff may also be unreliable, even when the wording sounds confident.

A search feature can reduce this limitation. After receiving a question, the system can search the web or internal documents, read the results, and use that newly retrieved material in its answer. It is no longer relying only on what was learned during training.

When asking about current facts, check whether search is available. If it is not, independently verify any answer to a question whose correct response can change with the date.

steps.title: How training data shapes answers
steps.contentMarkdown:
What developers include in the training data, and how much of it they use, affects both the content and depth of a model’s answers.

If the model was trained on far more English material, the same question may receive a more detailed answer in English. Topics documented mainly in Korean, such as modern Korean history or domestic institutions, may be explained less accurately or with less specificity.

Coverage also varies by field. A topic with abundant writing on the open internet is more likely to receive a detailed answer. A subject found mostly in academic papers or paid sources may get only a basic explanation.

To judge these limits, inspect the details. Look for names, years, and event titles, then verify each one directly. If the response continues in vague generalities without concrete facts, the model may not have had enough relevant training material.

quiz.question: Why does the same mistake come back in a new conversation?
choices: The feature that saves corrections is switched off
Nothing inside the model changes during inference
The model judged the correction to be wrong
Conversation logs are encrypted and cannot be read
quiz.explanation: The moment a user is typing is inference. The values inside the model are fixed then, so a correction stays alive only inside the context of that conversation.

quiz.question: Which situation describes overfitting?
choices: Scores are high on the material used for learning but drop on material the model has not seen
Scores are evenly high on both the learning material and new material
Training runs far too slowly
The model is too large to store
quiz.explanation: Overfitting means the material got memorized instead of the method learned. You spot it when the score on learning material and the score on new material come apart.

quiz.question: What is the safest choice when asking about facts from after the knowledge cutoff?
choices: Ask the same question several times in a row
Request a longer answer
Work in a setup with search or document lookup and take the sources along with the answer
Switch the question to English
quiz.explanation: Events past the cutoff are not inside the model. It is safer to work where the system reads retrieved material to answer, and to receive the sources so you can check them.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: How Neural Networks Calculate and Learn
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: A neural network multiplies and adds inputs, filters the results, and passes them through layers. During training, it gradually adjusts its weights to reduce the error between its answers and the correct ones.
objectives: Explain the calculation performed by a single artificial neuron.
Explain why neural networks use multiple layers.
Understand neural-network training as a process of adjusting weights.

steps.title: How neural networks calculate
steps.contentMarkdown:
Researchers borrowed the name **neural network** from the nerve cells of the brain. The borrowing stops at the name. Neural networks were not designed to reproduce the brain, whose workings are still not fully understood.

What happens inside is mostly multiplication and addition. A unit takes in several numbers, multiplies each by a different value, and adds the results. It then filters that total before passing it to the next stage. This single computational unit is called an **artificial neuron**.

Researchers had already proposed this approach in the 1950s. At the time, computers were too weak and there was too little training material. Once both computing power and data became available in the 2010s, neural networks came back into wide use.

They are sometimes described as thinking like people. In practice, they perform a great deal of arithmetic in a fixed structure.

steps.title: How an artificial neuron processes inputs
steps.contentMarkdown:
An artificial neuron receives several inputs and multiplies each one by a **weight**. A weight is a number that determines how strongly an input affects the calculation. The neuron adds the weighted values, then adds one more value that acts as a threshold. Finally, it sends the result through an **activation function** to determine what passes to the next stage.

Think about reviewing a loan application. The reviewer considers income, length of employment, and existing debt. Since these factors do not matter equally, income might receive a large weight and length of employment a smaller one. Multiply each score by its weight, add the results, and approve the loan if the total clears the threshold.

The activation function filters the calculation by a fixed rule. One common form turns negative values into zero and lets positive values pass unchanged. Without this step, even many stacked layers could be reduced to one simple sequence of multiplication and addition. Activation functions let the network handle problems that cannot be separated by a single straight line.

steps.title: Why neural networks use multiple layers
steps.contentMarkdown:
Developers place many artificial neurons side by side and feed their results into the next row as inputs. Each row is called a **layer**. One neuron can make only a simple distinction, but several layers can distinguish increasingly complex features. The term **deep learning** comes from building networks with many layers.

When a network is trained to recognize faces, different layers process different features.

- First layer: boundaries between light and dark, short lines
- Middle layers: corners, curves, and textures formed from lines
- Later layers: facial parts such as eyes, nose, and mouth
- Final layer: a person's identity, inferred from the arrangement of those parts

Nobody separately instructs a middle layer to `find the eyes`. Developers build multiple layers and repeatedly train the network to produce the correct answer. As a result, calculations that respond to features such as eyes or noses emerge in the middle layers. Early layers process simple lines, while later ones distinguish more complex objects.
steps.imageAlt: A simple edge shadow passing through four physical mesh layers and assembling into a face on the final wall

steps.title: How learning adjusts weights
steps.contentMarkdown:
Developers initially fill a neural network with meaningless weight values. Feed it a photo in this state and it will usually produce a wildly incorrect answer. Reaching the correct answer requires revising those weights again and again.

Training repeats the following process.

1. Feed in an input and calculate an answer.
2. Measure the error between that answer and the correct one.
3. Adjust the weights slightly in the direction that reduces the error.
4. Move to the next input and repeat.

In step 3, the calculation moves backward from the final layer to determine how much each weight affected the error. This process is called **backpropagation**.

Changing the weights too much at once can overshoot a better value and make the calculations keep swinging. That is why the adjustments are small. The amount changed at each step is the **learning rate**, one of several settings chosen by a person.

As this process is repeated across many inputs, the weights gradually change and the error falls.

steps.title: Why model decisions are hard to explain
steps.contentMarkdown:
After training, the adjusted weights remain inside the model. A large model can contain more than billions of them.

Viewed alone, each weight looks like a number with no special meaning. It is difficult to explain in words why any one of them settled on its particular value. Nor can a person select a few factors and present them as the basis for the decision, as in saying that income carries a large weight in a loan review. The model's judgment is distributed across billions of values.

As a result, a model may produce accurate answers without clearly explaining why. That can be a problem in medicine, hiring, and lending, where the basis for a decision may need to be disclosed.

Researchers are analyzing these internal calculations by checking which neurons respond to particular concepts. For now, they can explain only parts of the process. People still cannot read the entire chain of judgments that leads a model to its answer.

quiz.question: What does a single artificial neuron compute?
choices: It compares the inputs against each other and keeps only the largest
It multiplies each input by a weight, adds the results, and passes them through an activation function
It looks each input up in a dictionary and substitutes the meaning
It shuffles the inputs at random and hands them to the next layer
quiz.explanation: It multiplies by weights, sums the products, adds a threshold value, then filters the result through an activation function on the way to the next layer. Without that filter, stacked layers collapse into a single multiplication.

quiz.question: In a face recognition network, how do the early layers differ from the later ones in what they pick up?
choices: The early layers see only color and the later ones only size
The early layers handle simple fragments such as lines and edges, the later ones complex concepts such as parts and identity
The early and later layers repeat exactly the same work
The early layers are specified by a person and the later ones settled by learning
quiz.explanation: As layers go deeper they climb from simple fragments toward complex concepts. Which layer takes which role is not specified by a person but settled during training.

quiz.question: Why are weights not moved by a large amount in a single step?
choices: Because it costs more to compute
Because storage would run short
Because it overshoots the point of lowest error and the values swing around
Because weights must never turn negative
quiz.explanation: A large step jumps past the point where the error is smallest, so the values never settle. The learning rate is kept small and the weights are pushed into place gradually.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Turning Text into Tokens and Numbers
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: AI models split text into tokens and turn those tokens into numerical coordinates for computation. This process affects cost, capacity, and the kinds of mistakes models often make.
objectives: Explain why models need tokens and why token counts differ across languages.
Describe how embeddings represent the meaning of tokens as numerical coordinates.
Anticipate token-related mistakes and adjust requests to reduce them.

steps.title: Why models split text into tokens
steps.contentMarkdown:
A neural network multiplies and adds. It accepts nothing but numbers, so what a user types must first be divided into units and assigned numerical IDs.

The simplest approach would number every character. For example, `a` could be 1 and `b` could be 2. But this makes sentences extremely long, while each unit carries very little information.

Numbering every word creates the opposite problem. A complete list cannot easily accommodate new coinages, typos, and proper nouns. Words missing from the list could not be processed.

The practical middle ground is to bundle character fragments that frequently appear together. Each unit is called a **token**. A token is usually larger than one character and smaller than one word, although a common word may form a single token.

steps.title: Why token counts differ by language
steps.contentMarkdown:
Tokens are chosen from character combinations that appear frequently in the material used to train a model. Because that material has included large amounts of English, common English words often fit into a single token.

Korean can require several times as many tokens to express the same meaning. Particles and endings attach to words, continually changing their written forms. The splitting rules have also been strongly shaped by English-language data.

That difference affects real usage.

- Services that charge by token may cost more for the same content in Korean.
- The amount a model can read at once is measured in tokens. Under the same limit, less Korean text will fit.
- Output limits are also measured in tokens, so a Korean response may be cut off sooner.

Requesting the same task in English can sometimes reduce cost and processing time. If the final result must be in Korean, however, a person may need to revise its wording and tone.

steps.title: How embeddings represent meaning
steps.contentMarkdown:
The ID attached to a token is only an index. Token 3 and token 4 may have nearby numbers without having similar meanings.

The model therefore converts each token into coordinates made up of hundreds or thousands of numbers. This numerical list is called an **embedding**.

During training, tokens with related meanings move toward nearby positions. King and queen, Seoul and Tokyo, and run and sprint end up close together. No person assigns each position by hand. The model adjusts them as it learns from many sentences.

This property also supports searches based on meaning. Older search systems often needed the characters in a query to match the text being searched. Embeddings can treat `cheap laptop` and `affordable notebook computer` as nearby expressions, allowing both to appear even when their wording differs.
steps.imageAlt: Related porcelain miniatures clustered on emerald felt with an unrelated boat isolated far away

steps.title: How embeddings encode relationships
steps.contentMarkdown:
Models can use embedding coordinates to calculate relationships between words. Early embedding research tested these relationships by adding and subtracting coordinates.

One example became famous. Take king, subtract man, and add woman, and the result lands near queen. Take Paris, subtract France, and add Japan, and the result moves close to Tokyo. Relationships such as gender or the link between a country and its capital appeared as consistent differences between coordinates.

These calculations do not work precisely for every word. A few successful examples became widely known, but results often break down when several meanings and relationships are tangled together. An embedding is not a dictionary that organizes every meaning perfectly.

Modern models also represent the same token differently according to context. Surrounding words determine whether bank refers to the edge of a river or a place that holds money. The structure that adjusts a representation to fit its context is called **attention**.

steps.title: Mistakes caused by token processing
steps.contentMarkdown:
Because a model processes tokens instead of inspecting text one character at a time, it can fail at seemingly simple tasks.

**Counting characters:** A model may miscount how many times a character appears in a word. When the word is stored as one token or several fragments, the individual characters inside those tokens are difficult to inspect.

**Reversing text and word-chain games:** Reversing character order or isolating the final character is weak for the same reason. Both operations require separating characters that have been bundled together.

**Arithmetic:** Long numbers may be split across several tokens, making place values difficult to handle accurately. A calculator or executed code is safer.

**Unusual spellings:** Text containing special characters, severe typos, or rarely used foreign words may split into unfamiliar fragments. The result can become unstable.

For character work, separate the input with spaces, as in `a b c`. When counting or calculation is required, ask the model to perform it with code to reduce errors.

quiz.question: Why does the same content take more tokens in Korean than in English?
choices: Because Korean carries more information per sentence than English
Because the token splitting rules were derived from English material
Because Korean characters were added to Unicode later
Because Korean requires the embedding to be computed twice
quiz.explanation: Token units are set from the fragments that appeared often in training material. English material dominated, so the split is efficient for English, while Korean with its attached particles and endings breaks into finer pieces.

quiz.question: What is the key property of an embedding?
choices: It sorts tokens into alphabetical order
Tokens close in meaning end up close together in the coordinate space
It compresses tokens to save storage
It attaches one correct answer to each token
quiz.explanation: An embedding turns a token into a list of numbers, that is, into coordinates. During training, tokens close in meaning settle near one another, and that property is what made search by meaning possible.

quiz.question: Why do questions about how many times a letter appears in a word go wrong so often?
choices: Because the model cannot perform arithmetic at all
Because the question is too short
Because the word is already bundled into a token, so the letters inside are not visible one by one
Because counting letters is a forbidden operation
quiz.explanation: The model sees input as tokens rather than characters. When a whole word forms one chunk, counting the individual letters inside it is difficult.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: How Attention Powers Transformer Language Models
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Attention determines context by calculating relationships among the words in a sentence. This lesson explains how transformers use attention to process language and how parallel computation made larger models possible.
objectives: Explain with an example how attention processes context
Compare how RNNs and transformers process sentences
Understand how parallel processing enabled models to grow

steps.title: How attention finds context
steps.contentMarkdown:
Understanding context requires knowing which surrounding words matter to the word currently being processed.

`Daniel handed the book to his brother. He studied the cover for a long time.`

In the second sentence, **he** refers to the brother. The situation makes the connection natural: the person who received the book is the one studying its cover.

A machine cannot identify that person from **he** alone. It must decide which words in the previous sentence the pronoun connects to, and the answer changes with the sentence.

**Attention** calculates how much the current token should draw on every other token. When processing **he**, it gives brother a high weight and book a low one. These weights do not come from a fixed table. They are calculated again each time a sentence is processed.
steps.imageAlt: A triangular scene just after Minsu hands his brother a blank book, with only the brother studying the cover

steps.title: How attention calculates weights
steps.contentMarkdown:
Attention creates three values for every token: a **query**, a **key**, and **content**. The query is used to search for relevant tokens, the key helps determine relevance, and the content holds the information that will actually be retrieved.

The current token's query is compared with the keys of all the other tokens. A strong match receives a high weight. Attention then uses those weights to mix and retrieve the tokens' content. It works much like entering a search term in a library catalog and seeing the most relevant materials first.

Several versions of this calculation run at the same time. One may focus on grammatical relationships, another on what a pronoun refers to, and another on the main topic. This is called **multi-head attention**.

People do not assign each head a role in advance. During training, the model learns which relationships each head will focus on.

steps.title: How RNNs and transformers differ
steps.contentMarkdown:
Before transformers, language models commonly used **recurrent neural networks (RNNs)**, which processed a sentence one word at a time from beginning to end. At each step, the model updated a running summary with information from the next word.

This approach had two weaknesses.

- Information from the beginning became less distinct as sentences grew longer.
- Each word had to be processed before the next, making it difficult to divide the computation into simultaneous tasks.

The **transformer**, published in 2017, removed the recurrent structure and processed sentences with attention. It lays out all the tokens at once and allows each one to draw on the information it needs. The first word can refer directly to the last.

Attention alone cannot distinguish the order of words. To supply that information, a value indicating each token's position is added to its embedding.

steps.title: How parallel processing enabled larger models
steps.contentMarkdown:
Transformers can calculate information for many tokens at the same time. This **parallel processing** makes it easier to spread the work across multiple computing devices.

An RNN must finish one step before beginning the next. Even if a hundred machines are connected, each stage still has to wait its turn. A transformer processes the whole sentence at once, so adding more equipment can increase computation speed.

Researchers used this advantage to increase both the amount of training material and the size of models. They observed a tendency for performance to improve when the material grew tenfold and the model also grew tenfold, fueling competition to build larger models.

Computational cost remains a problem. Attention compares every token with every other token, so the work rises quickly as a sentence grows. Processing long documents is therefore expensive, and researchers continue to develop ways to reduce that cost.

steps.title: Practical limits of attention
steps.contentMarkdown:
Understanding attention helps explain problems that arise when writing requests or supplying long documents to AI systems.

**Put important conditions near the beginning or end.** A condition buried in the middle of a long request may not be reflected properly. Place any requirement that must be followed at the start or the end.

**Long documents sharply increase time and cost.** As the token count rises, the amount of computation grows at close to the square of that number. If the whole document is unnecessary, provide only the relevant sections.

**Reduce ambiguous references.** Expressions such as `it` or `the thing mentioned above` can lead the model to draw on the wrong information. Repeating the specific name makes a mistaken connection less likely.

After working out the context, the model builds its response by selecting the next token one at a time.

quiz.question: What does attention do?
choices: It deletes unnecessary words from the sentence
It computes how much the token being processed should draw on each of the other tokens
It sorts the words into alphabetical order
It fixes the length of the sentence in advance
quiz.explanation: Attention computes how much the tokens should draw on one another. Those weights do not come from a fixed table but are computed fresh for every sentence.

quiz.question: Where does the transformer part ways with the earlier recurrent approach?
choices: It reads the words one at a time in order, front to back
It lays the whole sentence out at once and lets the tokens reference each other
It runs on rules alone with no training
It has no limit on sentence length whatsoever
quiz.explanation: The recurrent approach read front to back while updating a running summary. The transformer drops the recurrence, handles the whole sentence at once, and has the tokens reference each other directly.

quiz.question: Why do cost and time rise sharply when a long document is fed in?
choices: Because the document gets read through several times over
Because every token is matched against every other token, so computation swells steeply as length grows
Because long documents use separate storage
Because an extra translation step gets added
quiz.explanation: Attention matches every token against every other token, so the amount of computation grows close to the square of the length. Excerpting only the part that matters pays off.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: How AI Generates Answers One Token at a Time
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Generative AI builds an answer by choosing one token at a time based on everything written so far. How it selects among candidates affects both the variety and consistency of the result.
objectives: Explain how AI builds an answer by repeatedly predicting the next token.
Distinguish how temperature affects accuracy, consistency, and variety.
Explain why the same prompt can produce different answers and how to reduce those differences.

steps.title: AI predicts the next token
steps.contentMarkdown:
Generative AI does not decide on a complete answer in advance. It looks only at the input and the text written so far, then calculates **the probability of the next token**. A token may be a single character, a whole word, or part of a word.

The model selects one candidate and appends it, making the text one token longer. It then uses that longer text to calculate the next set of probabilities. The process repeats until the model produces a signal that the answer should end.

While writing the first sentence, it does not yet know what the last sentence will be. Still, each selected token narrows the candidates that can plausibly follow, so the result usually holds together.

The way an answer appears on screen one character or word at a time is not merely a visual effect. The answer is genuinely being built by selecting tokens in sequence.
steps.imageAlt: A mosaic artisan placing one tile at the end of a finished path with an unplanned blank floor and candidate pieces ahead

steps.title: Each candidate has a different probability
steps.contentMarkdown:
The model gives every possible next token a different probability. After `The weather today is`, for example, the candidates might look like this.

| Candidate | Probability |
|---|---|
| fine | High |
| cloudy | Medium |
| cold | Medium |
| rectangular | Near zero |

Across the full vocabulary, most tokens have probabilities near zero. A small number that fit the context divide most of the probability among them.

Always choosing the highest-probability candidate tends to produce safe sentences. It can also make the wording predictable or cause the same phrase to repeat.

Selecting candidates randomly according to their probabilities creates more variety, but it also increases the chance of drawing something that fits the context less well. Services and developers adjust settings to strike a balance between stability and variety.

steps.title: Temperature controls output variety
steps.contentMarkdown:
**Temperature** is a common setting for controlling randomness when the next token is selected. It determines how strongly the model concentrates on candidates with high probabilities.

- Lowering the temperature makes high-probability candidates more likely to be selected. The output becomes more stable, which suits translation, summarization, data extraction, and code, where accuracy matters.
- Raising the temperature gives lower-probability candidates a greater chance of being selected. This can produce more varied results for brainstorming or creating several drafts. If the temperature is too high, sentences may become awkward or the content may lose coherence.

Other settings restrict the candidate pool itself. Common methods include keeping only a few of the highest-probability candidates or adding candidates from highest probability downward until their cumulative probability reaches a set share.

Consumer interfaces usually hide these settings and use values chosen by the service. Developer connections may allow temperature and the candidate range to be specified directly.

steps.title: The same prompt can produce different answers
steps.contentMarkdown:
The same question can produce a different answer each time because randomness enters when the next token is selected. If the model chooses a different token at any point, the text available as context also changes, and the rest of the answer can follow another path.

This variation can be a problem when:

- The same fields must be extracted from the same material on every run.
- Test or validation results must be checked repeatedly.
- Several people need to receive the same result.

With a developer connection, lowering the temperature can reduce randomness, and the same starting seed can be specified. Even then, identical results are not guaranteed. Differences may still arise from computation order or changes made by the service.

Restricting the output format can reduce variation further. Define the table cells or fields in advance, or require the model to answer only `yes` or `no`. A narrower range of valid choices leaves less room for the outputs to diverge.

steps.title: Limits of next-token prediction
steps.contentMarkdown:
Repeatedly predicting the next token is powerful for producing natural sentences, but it has limits when managing the overall structure of a long piece.

**Sentence flow is strong.** The model has practiced predicting what comes next countless times, so it can continue with expressions that fit the surrounding context.

**The overall structure can slip.** Because the conclusion and full organization are not fixed before writing begins, a long response may become logically inconsistent or forget a condition stated near the start. One way to reduce this problem is to ask for an outline first, then provide that outline again when requesting the full text.

**An early error can carry through the answer.** Each token is chosen from what has already been written. If a false premise appears early, later content may continue to build on it. You should not expect the model to notice the mistake midway and automatically start over.

Hallucinations, in which the model gives plausible but false information, are also related to this process. AI is not inherently a fact-lookup system. It builds an answer by continuing with tokens that are likely to fit the context.

quiz.question: How does a generative model build an answer?
choices: It computes the entire answer in one pass and returns it
It scores the probability of the next token, picks one, appends it, and repeats
It retrieves the closest match from answers stored in advance
It builds the sentence backward, from the end to the beginning
quiz.explanation: The single calculation the model performs is scoring the probability of the next token. It picks one, appends it, and feeds the now longer text back in for the same calculation.

quiz.question: Which setting suits work that extracts fields from source material accurately?
choices: Raise the temperature to widen the range of candidates
Lower the temperature so weight concentrates on high-probability candidates
Change the temperature at random across several runs
The result is the same regardless of temperature
quiz.explanation: Lowering the temperature sharpens the distribution and stabilizes the output. That suits translation, summarizing, and data extraction, where accuracy matters.

quiz.question: Why does the internal logic of a long piece come apart so easily?
choices: Because long pieces were absent from the training material
Because it appends the next phrase as it goes instead of fixing a conclusion in advance
Because a cap on the number of sentences is in force
Because the spell checker is not running
quiz.explanation: The model appends one token after another rather than laying out an overall design first. Long pieces can therefore drop an earlier condition or drift out of logic, which is why asking for an outline first helps.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Why AI Hallucinates and How to Verify Answers
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: AI can present invented sources and quotations as if they were real. Learn why hallucinations occur, which questions invite them, and how to verify the answers you receive.
objectives: Explain how AI generates answers and why that process can produce hallucinations.
Recognize questions that are especially likely to trigger hallucinations.
Build a process for verifying sources and factual claims provided by AI.

steps.title: How AI invents sources
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI can produce a paper title, an author, and a publication year in a single line even when the paper does not exist. The format may look completely natural. It may even use the name of a real journal or researcher, yet the paper itself appears nowhere.

The same thing happens with court decisions, book page numbers, statistics, and interview quotes. This effect is called **hallucination**.

It is different from a human lie. AI has no intent to deceive and no awareness that it has produced something nonexistent. It has simply generated a plausible answer that fits the question.

Tone gives nothing away. Accurate and invented answers can sound equally calm and confident, so wording alone cannot tell you which one you received.
steps.imageAlt: A grand academic archive illusion revealed from the side as a thin painted stage flat with empty space behind it

steps.title: How AI predicts what comes next
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI does not answer by searching through a stored list of facts. It calculates which words are likely to come next based on the text that came before.

After a phrase like `according to a study published in 2019`, something shaped like a paper title is likely to follow. AI produces language that fits that slot, but it does not separately check whether the paper exists.

Facts are not stored as individual entries, either. They are distributed across many weights. Information that appeared often in the training material may be reproduced fairly accurately, while rare facts can blend with similar information.

That is why AI may correctly name a famous person's best-known work but get details of a lesser-known person's career wrong. It cannot clearly distinguish what it knows from what it does not.

steps.title: Which questions invite hallucination
steps.contentMarkdown:
Hallucination becomes more likely when a question asks for details that are difficult to verify. Take extra care when several of these conditions overlap.

- **You ask for a specific identifier.** Paper titles, case numbers, page numbers, exact dates, and quotations all require direct confirmation.
- **Little relevant material is available.** Training data may be thin for local figures, small organizations, one country's institutions, or details of an old event.
- **The question assumes something nonexistent.** If a prompt includes a false concept or event, AI may invent an explanation instead of correcting the premise.
- **You ask about events after the knowledge cutoff.** AI may connect unknown recent information to older knowledge and answer as though it knows.
- **You demand a long list.** If only six supported examples exist but you request ten, AI may fill in the remaining four.

Fixed list lengths are especially risky. Instead of saying `give me ten`, ask for `only the examples whose evidence you can verify`.

steps.title: Why search results still need verification
steps.contentMarkdown:
Search and document lookup can greatly reduce hallucination because AI can base its answer on material it has just found rather than relying on recall. Errors can still remain.

- If it retrieves an inaccurate blog post or faulty document, it may repeat the error as written.
- While summarizing a source, it may add a causal relationship that the original never claimed or omit an important condition.
- It may provide an address that looks like supporting evidence, only for the link to contain different information or lead to a missing page.

When AI provides a source, **open the link yourself and confirm that the claimed information is actually there.** Do not stop at the page title. Find the relevant passage in the body and check its conditions as well. Skipping this step cuts the benefit of search in half.

steps.title: How to verify an AI answer
steps.contentMarkdown:
Anecdotes and quotations produced by AI should be compared with other materials before you use them. The same standard applies when working with biographical information or quoted language.

- **Delegate only what you can verify.** If you have no way to check claims in a field, do not entrust the entire fact-checking process to AI.
- **Confirm identifiers in the original source.** Check titles, years, page numbers, and case numbers directly in the source material.
- **Rephrase the question and ask again.** If the answer changes substantially when the same question is worded differently, its basis may be weak.
- **Tell AI to admit when it does not know.** Add a condition such as `If you cannot verify it, do not guess. Say that you do not know.`

No single setting can eliminate hallucination. Important facts and sources still require separate human verification.

quiz.question: What is the underlying reason hallucination occurs?
choices: False information is mixed into the training material
The structure continues a plausible next phrase with no step that looks facts up
It only happens when the internet connection drops
The user asked a difficult question
quiz.explanation: The model is not a fact lookup system but one that computes the probability of the next token. It produces a string that fits the slot, and no step confirming that the thing exists sits in the structure.

quiz.question: Which request carries the highest risk of hallucination?
choices: Asking for an explanation of a widely known concept
Asking for a sentence to be tightened up
Asking for exactly ten accurate references on a little known topic
Asking for the spelling in a piece of writing to be fixed
quiz.explanation: Risk peaks where thin material, specific identifiers, and a pinned item count overlap. The model tends to fill the count even when the basis runs short.

quiz.question: What check still remains even for an answer produced with search attached?
choices: Ask for the answer again at greater length
Open the cited links directly and confirm the content is there
Repeat the same question ten times
Translate the answer into another language
quiz.explanation: Retrieved material can be wrong, a summary can drift from the original, and a link can be formatted correctly but lead nowhere. Skipping the step of opening the source cuts the benefit of search.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Why Conversational AI Speaks Differently
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Conversational AI is shaped through pretraining, fine-tuning, and preference tuning. These stages explain why services built on the same base model can speak differently and draw different refusal lines.
objectives: Distinguish the roles of pretraining, fine-tuning, and preference tuning.
Explain why services built from the same base model can develop different characters.
Recognize the side effects of human preference tuning and reduce them with specific prompts.

steps.title: The three stages of conversational model training
steps.contentMarkdown:
Conversational models are built through three stages in sequence: **pretraining, fine-tuning, and preference tuning**. Each teaches a different set of abilities and responses.

| Stage | What it does | What the model learns |
|---|---|---|
| Pretraining | Predicts the next token across vast amounts of text | Feel for language, knowledge of the world |
| Fine-tuning | Learns from paired instructions and model answers | How to respond to a request |
| Preference tuning | Learns from answers that people judge better | Tone, refusal thresholds, safety judgment |

Pretraining consumes most of the time and money. Fine-tuning and preference tuning are smaller by comparison, yet they are largely responsible for the tone and behavior users notice.

The model acquires its knowledge and language ability during pretraining. The later stages shape how it conducts an actual conversation and give the finished service its character.
steps.imageAlt: One pottery workshop arranged continuously from basic forming to functional refinement to selection of the finished vessel

steps.title: What pretraining teaches
steps.contentMarkdown:
Pretraining feeds the model enormous quantities of text, including web pages, books, encyclopedias, and code, and asks it to predict the next token. No one has to label the correct answer separately. The text already supplies it as the token that comes next.

A model that finishes this stage can continue sentences naturally. It is not yet easy to use as a conversation partner. Ask it a question and, instead of answering, it may produce more similar questions because online text often places one question after another.

Knowledge enters at this stage too. The model learns frequent material well and may not learn rare material thoroughly. The latest point represented in the training data also helps determine its knowledge cutoff.

A model with language ability and knowledge, but without training to respond properly to requests, is called a **base model**.

steps.title: What fine-tuning changes
steps.contentMarkdown:
Fine-tuning uses examples that pair an instruction with a model answer. Across many such pairs, the model learns how different kinds of requests should be answered.

After fine-tuning, it answers questions, follows requested formats, and explains complex ideas step by step. Its store of knowledge does not grow dramatically. What changes is how it brings out what it learned during pretraining and applies it to the request at hand.

This stage also teaches a tone suited to a particular use. Add legal documents to the same base model and it will use legal phrasing more often. Add counseling material and its voice will sound more like a counselor's. Companies use the same method to create internal models.

Services built on one base model can therefore respond in very different ways. Their fine-tuning data differs even when their foundation is identical.

steps.title: How human preferences shape responses
steps.contentMarkdown:
During preference tuning, people compare several answers to the same question and choose the better one. The model uses those choices to learn the qualities people tend to prefer.

This is where services can diverge in several visible ways.

- **Tone:** Whether the voice is stiff or warm
- **Answer length:** Whether it explains in detail or answers briefly
- **Refusal thresholds:** How far it answers and where it stops
- **Expressions of uncertainty:** Whether it sounds certain or admits that it does not know
- **Format habits:** Whether it favors lists or explains in paragraphs

The company decides what counts as a better answer. Evaluators choose according to those standards, and the model learns the tone and judgment behind the selected responses.

Ask several services the same question and their core answers may be similar while their attitudes differ. That gap often reflects different preference-tuning criteria.

steps.title: Side effects of preference tuning
steps.contentMarkdown:
What people prefer is not always the same as what is accurate or appropriate. As a result, tuning a model to human preferences can produce several side effects.

**It may agree too readily.** When a user begins with a false premise, the model may go along instead of correcting it. This tendency can emerge when evaluators favor answers that agree with them.

**It may become more cautious than necessary.** The model may refuse harmless requests or attach so many warnings that the main answer gets lost.

**It may favor long, formal answers.** Even a question that could be answered briefly may receive lists, subheadings, and a lengthy explanation.

Specific instructions can reduce these tendencies. Try prompts such as `Point out any false premise in my question`, `State how confident you are`, or `Answer in three sentences`. Directly requesting disagreement, confidence, or a fixed length helps override the model's defaults.

quiz.question: What state is a base model in after pretraining finishes?
choices: Ready to use as a conversation partner that answers questions directly
Good at continuing sentences but not in the shape of answering a request
Without knowledge but already in conversational form
Fully finished, with human preferences already folded in
quiz.explanation: Pretraining installs a feel for language and knowledge through next-token prediction. The shape of answering a request appears in the next stage, fine-tuning.

quiz.question: Why do services with entirely different characters come out of the same base model?
choices: Because pretraining is redone from scratch for each service
Because the material layered on and the criteria used differ at the fine-tuning and preference tuning stages
Because each service splits text into tokens differently
Because the servers sit in different locations
quiz.explanation: Expensive pretraining builds the foundation, and character is settled in the two later stages. Different layered material and different preference criteria yield different characters from the same foundation.

quiz.question: What side effect comes out of folding in human preferences?
choices: Knowledge disappears
Sentences stop being grammatical
It leans toward agreeing with the user and answers run longer than needed
It loses the ability to handle other languages
quiz.explanation: The answer people rate highly and the accurate answer do not always coincide. An agreeable posture, excessive caution, and long formal formatting are left behind as defaults.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: The Four Elements of an AI Prompt
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Effective AI requests specify the context, task, format, and constraints. Understanding these four elements helps you revise a prompt until it produces the result you need.
objectives: Identify and write the context, task, format, and constraints in a prompt.
Predict how changing a request will change the AI's response.
Find missing elements and revise a prompt to make it more specific.

steps.title: Specify the missing information
steps.contentMarkdown:
Type `Write a blog post` and you will get something general enough for almost anyone. If you do not name the reader, the AI assumes an average reader. If you leave out the length, it chooses something in the middle. The more information you omit, the more the AI has to guess.

Try a more specific request:

`This is a science blog for middle school students. Explain photosynthesis in about 400 words. Use three subheadings and exactly one analogy. Do not use chemical formulas.`

Now the reader, length, structure, and prohibitions are fixed. A good prompt does not depend on clever phrasing. It **reduces the information the AI has to guess**.

steps.title: The four elements of a prompt
steps.contentMarkdown:
A prompt can include **context, task, format, and constraints**. Sorting the necessary information into these four elements makes it easier to see what is missing.

| Element | What to include | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Context | Who will read it, why, and where it will be used | Science blog for middle schoolers, classroom handout |
| Task | What the AI should do | Write an explanation of how photosynthesis works |
| Format | The length and structure of the result | About 400 words, three subheadings, prose paragraphs |
| Constraints | Requirements and prohibitions | No chemical formulas, one analogy only |

You do not always need all four. A simple question may need only the task. When a response disappoints, look for the missing element and add it.

Context is especially easy to omit. You already know your situation and purpose, so it is tempting to assume the AI knows them too.
steps.imageAlt: An overhead fabrication bench physically integrating user, task, finished shell, and height limit in one child-scale sluice exhibit

steps.title: State the audience and purpose
steps.contentMarkdown:
Context tells the AI **who will read the result** and **how it will be used**. Even when the topic stays the same, the audience and purpose can change the vocabulary, level of explanation, and structure.

Write `An investment analyst will read this`, and the AI will address someone familiar with the field. Write `A college student encountering the topic for the first time will read this`, and it will begin by explaining unfamiliar concepts.

State the purpose as well. `This will open a presentation` encourages an opening line that draws in the audience. `This is an internal document` moves the conclusion and work-related information toward the beginning.

You can also assign a role, as in `You are an editor with twenty years of experience`. A role can shape tone and point of view, but it does not give the AI knowledge it did not already have. Naming the audience and purpose changes the result more reliably than assigning a role alone.

steps.title: Describe the task with a verb
steps.contentMarkdown:
Do not put only a topic in the task. Use a verb to state **what the AI must do**. Type `about remote work`, and the AI cannot tell whether you want an overview, a summary of opposing views, or a draft policy.

Make the action explicit:

- `List three advantages and three disadvantages of adopting remote work.`
- `Rebut the arguments against adopting remote work.`
- `Draft a remote work policy as numbered clauses.`

Changing the verb produces a different deliverable. Decide whether the job is to summarize, compare, draft, review, classify, translate, or extract.

Several tasks packed into one request can leave each response short and shallow. If you need a summary, a critique, and an alternative, split them into separate requests and submit them in sequence.

steps.title: State requirements and prohibitions
steps.contentMarkdown:
Constraints tell the AI **what it must do** and **what it must not do**. Excluding unwanted language or content in advance reduces the editing needed afterward.

Collect the constraints you use often so you can reuse them:

- `Leave out anything that cannot be verified, and say when you do not know.`
- `When you include a number or quotation, provide its source.`
- `Write only in prose paragraphs, with no subheadings or lists.`
- `Do not use inflated modifiers or end with an encouraging remark.`
- `Add nothing that is not in the source text.`

During training, AI develops a tendency to treat long, formal responses as desirable. If that is not what you want, name the language and formats to exclude directly in the prompt.

Keep a list of constraints suited to your work. For each new request, you can select and attach the ones you need.

quiz.question: Which one is not one of the four slots of a prompt?
choices: Context
Task
Model name
Constraints
quiz.explanation: The four slots are context, task, format, and constraints. Which model you happen to be using is not something you write inside the prompt.

quiz.question: What belongs in the context slot?
choices: Who reads it and what it will be used for
The character count of the answer
A list of expressions to avoid
How many times to repeat the request
quiz.explanation: Context is reader and purpose. Stating who reads it and what it is for moves the result more reliably than assigning a role.

quiz.question: What happens when one request asks for a summary, a critique, and an alternative together?
choices: All three come out more accurate
All three come out shallow, so splitting them into separate requests works better
Only the summary is produced and the rest is ignored
The request gets refused
quiz.explanation: Overlapping tasks split the attention and the space each one gets, so all three end up thin. Ask for them separately.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: How Much AI Can Read at Once
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: AI can consult only a limited amount of information at one time. Understanding that limit helps you divide long conversations and documents into manageable parts.
objectives: Explain what a context window is and what information it contains.
Divide a long document so that only the necessary material is provided.
Decide when to end an existing conversation and start a new one.

steps.title: What goes into the context window
steps.contentMarkdown:
A model produces answers using only the information within a fixed range. That range is the **context window**, and its size is measured in tokens.

A desk is a useful picture. The model can consult whatever is spread across the desk, but anything left in a drawer is invisible. When space is limited, not every document can be laid out at once.

The context window contains more than the question you typed.

- Instructions the service inserted ahead of you
- The conversation so far
- Text you pasted and the contents of attached files
- Material retrieved through search
- The answer being generated right now

All of this has to fit under the limit together. Limits differ by service and model, and they keep growing year over year. Even so, there is always a ceiling on how much a model can read at once.
steps.imageAlt: An archivist able to examine only the records on a small circular light table while the rest remain in closed cabinets

steps.title: What happens when the limit is exceeded
steps.contentMarkdown:
When a conversation gets too long, the model may stop consulting information from the beginning. You asked for a different tone and the old one comes back. A phrase you banned reappears.

Once the limit is exceeded, the earliest parts of the conversation are usually cut away. Some services do this quietly. The model can no longer see the removed material, so from its perspective, that material might as well never have been provided.

Problems can appear even when everything fits. Several experiments have found that models tend to miss information buried in the middle of a long context. They consult the beginning and end more reliably, while details in the middle can slip past them.

Put conditions that absolutely must hold near the beginning or end of your request. With long source material, paste the material first and place the task instructions last. This reduces the chance that the model will overlook what it needs to do.

steps.title: How to divide a long document
steps.contentMarkdown:
You do not always need to provide an entire long document. Adding far more information than the task requires can raise costs and reduce accuracy.

- **Excerpt the relevant sections.** Select the passages connected to your question. If you do not know which sections matter, provide the table of contents first and ask the model to identify them.
- **Process it in stages.** Request a summary of each chapter, then combine only those summaries and ask for an overall conclusion.
- **Mark the source boundaries.** Put dividers at the beginning and end, and clearly label which text is source material. This reduces the chance that the model will confuse the source with your instructions.
- **Restrict the answer to the source.** Add `Do not include anything that is not in the material below`.

That final instruction matters. Without it, the model may mix background knowledge into its answer even when that information never appeared in the document. For work that must evaluate only what the source says, the result then becomes difficult to trust.

steps.title: When to start a new conversation
steps.contentMarkdown:
A longer conversation does not always produce a better answer. Start a new one when you see signals like these:

- The rules you established at the beginning keep getting broken.
- You have pointed out the same problem at least twice and it still is not fixed.
- The discussion has moved to a completely different topic.
- Several failed attempts and incorrect drafts have accumulated.

Failed attempts are especially likely to pull later answers in the same direction. If three bad drafts remain in the conversation, the fourth may come out looking much like the ones before it.

Before starting fresh, collect only the settled conclusions and the conditions that must be followed. You can ask for a summary of the existing conversation and paste that summary into the new one. There is no need to carry over every unnecessary detour and failed attempt.

steps.title: How memory differs from the context window
steps.contentMarkdown:
A service remembering previous conversations does not increase how much the model can read at one time.

The service stores selected information you provided, then inserts it again when a later conversation begins. The model reads that stored information anew each time. Anything inserted this way still occupies part of the context window.

If too much is stored, less room may remain for the current task. An old memory can also conflict with what you are doing now and interfere with the answer.

Conversation does not change the inside of the model. What changes is which information the service saves and supplies again. Clear memories that are irrelevant to your current work, and keep only the conditions you will continue to need.

quiz.question: Which one does not sit inside the context window?
choices: The conversation up to this point
The body text of a document you pasted
The entire original training corpus
The answer being generated right now
quiz.explanation: Instructions, the conversation, pasted material, search results, and the answer in progress all share the context window. Training data is dissolved inside the model and never loaded into that window.

quiz.question: Why should conditions that must hold go at the front or the back of a request?
choices: Sentences at the edges are cheaper to process
Information placed in the middle of a long context is reported to get missed
There is a character limit that applies to the middle
Position makes no difference, so it is only a habit
quiz.explanation: Even under the ceiling, the middle of a long context blurs, and that has been observed across several experiments. Key conditions belong at one end or the other.

quiz.question: In a conversation where several failed attempts have piled up, what is worth doing?
choices: Repeat the same request in stronger language
Carry only the settled conclusions into a fresh conversation
Ask it to delete the front of the conversation
Ask for a longer answer and try again
quiz.explanation: Wrong attempts left in the context keep pulling the work their way. Summarizing the conclusions and moving them into a new conversation is faster.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Getting Better AI Results with Examples
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Examples can communicate tone and output structure more precisely than explanation alone. The key is knowing how to choose them, format them, and keep them from pushing the result in the wrong direction.
objectives: Pair input and output examples effectively.
Specify output length, structure, and formatting in concrete terms.
Identify and correct examples that distort the result.

steps.title: When examples are more precise than words
steps.contentMarkdown:
Describing a tone in words can become vague almost immediately. A request like `Not too stiff, but not too casual either. Keep it plain.` may mean something different to every reader.

One example is often more precise. Paste a paragraph you like and write `Match the tone of this paragraph.` The AI can then use its word choice, sentence length, and sentence endings as guides.

Supplying a few examples inside a request is called **few-shot prompting**. It does not retrain the AI. The examples guide its response only within that conversation.

Tone, table design, classification criteria, and ways of organizing material can all be tedious to describe in detail. When a condition is hard to put into words, showing an example is usually faster.
steps.imageAlt: A woodworking apprentice building a new stool frame to match the proportions of one finished asymmetric wooden stool

steps.title: Pairing input and output examples
steps.contentMarkdown:
Each example should pair an input with its intended output.

Write `Organize the information in the following format.` Then provide a pair such as `Input: review of the iPhone 15 / Output: product=iPhone 15, category=electronics, sentiment=positive`.

A few guidelines make the examples more reliable.

- **Use only two or three.** Too many examples consume much of the text the AI can consider at once. They may also make inputs unlike the examples harder to handle.
- **Choose different kinds.** Two contrasting examples are better than three similar ones. A positive case and a negative case, for instance, establish a broader standard.
- **Include a difficult case.** Show how an ambiguous input should be handled so the same judgment can carry over.
- **Check every answer carefully.** If an example contains an error, the AI may adopt that error as part of the rule.

steps.title: Specifying the output format
steps.contentMarkdown:
Leave the output format open and the response may take a different shape each time. One answer may include subheadings, while another turns a list into paragraphs. This happens because the AI includes a sampling step that selects the next expression from several candidates.

State the format in concrete terms.

- **Shape:** `Organize this as a table with three columns: item, evidence, and risk.`
- **Length:** `Keep each item to two sentences or fewer.`
- **Heading:** `Start each item with a one-line bold heading.`
- **First line:** `Output only the result, with no explanation or greeting.`

If a program will process the answer directly, the format must be fixed. A change in structure can break whatever comes next. In that situation, a completed format example is usually more reliable than conditions alone.

steps.title: How bad examples distort results
steps.contentMarkdown:
Examples exert a strong pull on the response. Poorly chosen ones can push the result in the wrong direction.

**Using only one type:** Show three positive cases and the AI may classify a later negative case as positive. Include contrasting types in the example set.

**Copying the wording:** A paragraph supplied to demonstrate tone may contribute specific phrases as well. Define the scope clearly: `Do not reuse the wording. Follow only the sentence length and tone.`

**Forcing content into a fixed format:** Material that does not belong in a table may still be squeezed into its cells. Add an open-ended column or allow supplementary notes below the table.

If the response resembles the original examples too closely, reduce the number of examples or replace them with examples of a different kind.

steps.title: Managing examples for repeated work
steps.contentMarkdown:
If you repeat the same kind of work, keep your frequently used examples and output formats in a separate document. You will not have to rebuild the request each time, and the results will vary less.

Three things are worth collecting.

- Two or three paragraphs that clearly show your voice
- A few output formats you use often
- A list of constraints that apply every time

This project follows the same practice. Each repeated task has its own specification document, which the AI reads before starting. The document preserves the standard, so a person does not have to remember and retype every condition.

Review old examples regularly. If your voice has changed but you keep supplying earlier paragraphs, the output will continue to follow the old style. When a result feels unlike your current work, first check whether the examples still match your standards.

quiz.question: What effect does few-shot prompting have on the model?
choices: The model learns the examples and keeps them permanently
They are consulted only inside that request and conversation, and the model itself does not change
The model's knowledge cutoff moves forward
Other users see the effect in their results too
quiz.explanation: Putting examples inside a request is not training. They are imitated within that context and nothing remains once the conversation ends.

quiz.question: What is the better way to choose examples?
choices: Include ten or more examples that resemble each other
Pick two or three that differ in character and include an awkward case
Include one easy example and nothing more
Skip examples and write a long description instead
quiz.explanation: Two or three cover it, and pairing different kinds with an ambiguous case is what communicates the criteria.

quiz.question: The wording from your tone example keeps appearing in the output. What do you do?
choices: Add more examples
State the scope: do not reuse the wording, take only sentence length and tone
Remove every format instruction
Ask for a longer answer
quiz.explanation: Examples act with force, so wording gets copied along with tone. Name the scope to borrow from, or swap in an example with a different character.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Setting the Order of Work for AI
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Demand a conclusion too early and important conditions or checks may get skipped. Specifying the order of work and adding checkpoints can make an AI’s answers more accurate and easier to verify.
objectives: Break a complex request into connected, verifiable steps
Request and approve a plan before asking for a full draft
Distinguish work that benefits from multiple steps from work that does not

steps.title: Why conditions should come before conclusions
steps.contentMarkdown:
A generative AI builds an answer by choosing the next `token`, meaning the next character or fragment of a word, based on the text that came before it. Once it starts with a conclusion, the rest can easily develop in a way that supports that conclusion. It rarely goes back and corrects an unchecked conclusion on its own.

Questions involving calculation or comparison often expose this problem. Ask for only the answer to a problem with three conditions, and the AI may overlook one while still producing something polished and plausible.

Specify the order instead.

`Check each condition one at a time, then write your conclusion.`

The written checks remain available as context when the conclusion is formed. Research has confirmed the value of this approach, and many services now perform parts of the checking process internally.

steps.title: How to divide work into ordered steps
steps.contentMarkdown:
When assigning several tasks at once, number the steps and state their order.

`Work in this order. 1) Pull and quote every relevant clause from the source. 2) Judge clause by clause whether it applies to our situation. 3) Collect only the clauses that apply and write the appropriate actions.`

This separates finding information from judging it. It also makes mistakes easier to trace. If the actions in step three look wrong, you can start by checking the clauses quoted in step one.

Follow three rules when dividing the work.

- **Give each step one job.** Asking the AI to extract and judge at the same time mixes two tasks.
- **Make later steps use earlier results.** A list of unrelated tasks does not improve accuracy.
- **Ask it to show intermediate results.** If those results stay hidden, you cannot tell where an error occurred.

steps.title: Why the plan should come before the draft
steps.contentMarkdown:
For a long report, proposal, or other substantial document, getting the plan before the full draft is safer.

`Do not write it yet. Give me the outline and what each section will cover. I will review that before you write the body.`

If the direction is wrong, reviewing the plan lets you correct a few lines. Discover the problem after the full text is written, and the entire document may need to be redone.

Check three things:

- Is the scope right?
- Is anything missing?
- Does the order flow naturally?
