If changes are needed, ask for the revised plan to be printed again. Pointing out corrections and immediately requesting the body can cause some of them to be missed. The updated plan needs to remain in the conversation as written context for the answer that follows.
steps.imageAlt: An engineer checking the joint sequence on a scale bridge model before work begins across the real empty span

steps.title: How to make AI review its own answer
steps.contentMarkdown:
After an AI produces an answer, use a separate request to make it look for problems.

`Mark the claims in the answer above that rest on weak support.`

`Pull only the sentences in the draft above that need fact-checking.`

`Argue against this conclusion from the opposing position.`

A follow-up in the same conversation treats the earlier answer as the material to review. The AI will not catch every flaw in its own writing, but a targeted review increases the chance of finding errors.

Avoid adding only a doubtful question such as `Is that right?` The AI may try to agree with your suspicion and change an answer that was already correct.

State exactly what it should check. Useful criteria include **whether claims have support**, **whether every stated condition was met**, and **whether any sentences require fact-checking**.

steps.title: When a task needs separate steps
steps.contentMarkdown:
Not every request needs to be divided into steps. More steps take additional time and cost to process.

Breaking the work apart is useful for:

- Judgments that must account for several conditions
- Work that extracts and organizes source material before reaching a conclusion
- Tasks combining calculation and comparison
- Long deliverables where structure matters

A direct request is usually enough for:

- Translation, spelling correction, or tone polishing
- Short fact checks
- Format conversion

Adding multiple stages to these simpler tasks often produces more explanation without materially changing the result. In those cases, ask: `Output the result only, with no explanation.`

Use a human workflow as the test. If a person would need intermediate notes, calculations, or organized findings to complete the task, put that sequence into the request.

quiz.question: Why is a request that demands the conclusion straight away a disadvantage?
choices: The answer comes out shorter
Once a conclusion is started, what follows gets written to support it, and the model cannot walk itself back
It costs more to run
The formatting falls apart
quiz.explanation: The model extends what it has already written. A conclusion produced without checking will not be reversed later, so put the checking in front of it.

quiz.question: Why take the plan first on a sizable piece of work?
choices: Plans are more accurate than bodies of text
A wrong direction can be corrected in a few lines
Plans cost nothing to produce
You no longer have to write the body
quiz.explanation: Drift found after the full text arrives means rewriting the whole thing. Caught at the plan stage, the cost of correction is far smaller.

quiz.question: Which task does not need to be split into steps?
choices: A judgment carrying several conditions
Extracting items from a source, organizing them, and reaching a conclusion
Correcting the spelling in a sentence
A review that mixes calculation and comparison
quiz.explanation: Work a person handles without scratch notes has no use for steps. Spelling correction and format conversion just gain a longer preamble.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: How to Revise AI Responses Part by Part
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Treat an AI’s first response as a draft, then revise only what needs work. Preserve what already works, and know when a fresh conversation will be more effective.
objectives: Request precise changes without rewriting the entire response.
Tell the AI which content and formatting it must preserve.
Decide whether to continue revising or start a new conversation.

steps.title: What to check in the first response
steps.contentMarkdown:
A single request rarely produces a finished response. Just as you would review and shape a draft from a person, treat an AI’s first answer as a draft.

Check the **information** before worrying about polish. The response shows how the AI understood your request. If it heads in a completely different direction, your original instructions may have left out an important condition.

Start with three questions.

- Was the task understood correctly?
- Did the response follow the requested format?
- Are the facts and supporting evidence sound?

If the task itself was misunderstood, add the missing conditions and start over. If the overall direction is right and only the format or facts are wrong, continue from the current response and revise those parts.

steps.title: Specify exactly what to change
steps.contentMarkdown:
Asking only `Rewrite it` can erase the parts that already work. Each new response may use different wording and organization, so the second paragraph you liked could disappear.

Instead of requesting a full rewrite, identify both the location and the problem.

- `Remove the statistic from the second paragraph and replace it with one example. Leave everything else unchanged.`
- `The last sentence sounds preachy. Replace it with a factual explanation.`
- `The third and fifth items repeat the same point. Merge them.`

The more precisely you name the target, the easier it is to preserve the surrounding text. If the location is difficult to describe, quote the sentence itself and state the change you want. That reduces the chance that the AI will edit the wrong passage.
steps.imageAlt: A conservator repairing only one small tear in an otherwise intact tapestry

steps.title: Specify what should stay
steps.contentMarkdown:
Even when you request one small change, the AI may also alter the tone or structure of nearby sentences. Along with what to revise, name **what must not change**.

- `Leave the first and last paragraphs exactly as they are.`
- `Keep the title and subheadings.`
- `Keep the overall length close to what it is now.`

After several rounds, earlier requirements can fade from the conversation. After about three exchanges, restate all the conditions you have settled on as a list.

For a long piece, you can also limit what the AI returns. `Rewrite only the third section. Do not print the rest.` This leaves less room for unrelated parts to be changed.

steps.title: Ask for options when direction is unclear
steps.contentMarkdown:
When you have not settled on a direction, ask for several options at the start and compare them. This works well for titles, openings, structures, and names.

For example: `Give me ten title candidates in different directions.` You can choose one candidate or combine the strongest parts of two.

A large number alone may produce a string of similar options. As the AI generates each candidate, the earlier ones can influence what follows. Add a condition such as `in different directions`, or divide the options into types yourself.

`Give me three each in explanatory, question, and quotation form.`

Once you know which direction you want, stop expanding the list. Choosing one option and revising it precisely is usually faster.

steps.title: When to start a new conversation
steps.contentMarkdown:
If you point out the same problem three times and it still is not fixed, stop revising and start a new conversation. Failed requests and responses remain in the context, which can lead the AI to repeat similar results.

Bring the useful decisions with you when you start fresh.

- List the requirements you have confirmed
- Include a paragraph you liked as an example
- State the results you do not want and the approaches that failed

The last point is especially important. If you do not explain what went wrong, the new conversation may produce the same kind of response.

When the result is nearly finished, editing the remainder yourself may be faster. If several rounds of requests would take longer than fixing the final few sentences directly, there is no need to keep asking.

quiz.question: Why is `Rewrite it` an expensive request?
choices: It costs twice as much to run
The parts that came out well are lost too, and the result can come back completely different
The exact same result repeats
Format instructions stop applying
quiz.explanation: A full rewrite throws away the parts you wanted to keep. Because candidates are sampled, what you liked may not come back at all.

quiz.question: How do you reduce changes to parts you never asked about?
choices: Ask for a longer answer
Name what should stay untouched, or narrow the range to be rewritten
Send the same request twice
Remove the format instructions
quiz.explanation: Stating what not to touch, or asking for one section only, leaves far less room for the rest to shift.

quiz.question: What must you carry into a new conversation?
choices: The complete transcript of the previous conversation
The settled requirements plus a record of what failed
The configuration values of the model you used
The timestamps of your requests
quiz.explanation: Without a record of the failed directions, the new conversation falls into the same hole. Move the settled conditions, the examples you liked, and the failure list together.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: How to Verify AI Answers
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Learn a practical routine for catching confident but incorrect AI answers. You will also distinguish work AI can assist with from decisions that require human verification.
objectives: Request evidence and check the original source yourself
Rephrase questions to test whether an answer remains consistent
Distinguish appropriate AI tasks from decisions AI should not make

steps.title: Why tone cannot tell you what is true
steps.contentMarkdown:
An accurate answer and an invented one can arrive in the same confident voice. AI does not necessarily recognize that it has made something up, so a wrong answer may sound every bit as assured as a correct one.

Verification therefore has to be a routine, not a feeling. Checking only the parts that look odd will miss errors. Even natural, convincing prose can contain false information.

Always check the following:

- Names of people and organizations, and titles of works
- Years, dates, figures, and percentages
- Quotations and their sources
- Statutes, regulations, and court decisions
- Links and document titles

Not every sentence needs the same scrutiny. Start by isolating names, numbers, quotations, legal information, and links. Comparing those against reliable sources cuts the workload substantially.
steps.imageAlt: A surveyor checking two equally convincing unmarked compasses against a noon meridian shadow

steps.title: How to request specific sources
steps.contentMarkdown:
Ask only for sources, and you may receive an answer that merely looks properly documented. Specify what evidence to provide and how to display it.

`After each claim, give the document name and the specific passage it rests on. Mark any claim you cannot support as no source found.`

The final instruction matters. Unless the AI has a way to acknowledge missing evidence, it may try to fill the gap with a source it invented.

If search is available, request links as well. Then **open each link and confirm that the cited statement is actually there.** Recognizing a document title and moving on does not count as checking the source.

Leave paywalled or inaccessible material marked as unverified. If you have not seen the original, do not treat the claim as confirmed.

steps.title: How to test an answer by rephrasing
steps.contentMarkdown:
Ask about the same subject in different ways to see how stable the answer is. When the evidence is solid, changing the wording should produce a similar response. When support is thin, details such as the year or the person involved may shift from one answer to the next.

Try these approaches:

- **Ask again in a new conversation.** In the same conversation, the AI may simply repeat an earlier answer because it remains in context.
- **Remove the assumption.** Instead of `A is said to have done B. Is that true?`, ask `What facts are established about the relationship between A and B?`
- **Include a false premise.** If the AI accepts and explains something that never happened instead of correcting it, its evidence may be weak.

Consistency does not prove correctness. A widely repeated error can produce the same wrong answer every time. Rephrasing is a useful test, but it never replaces checking the original source.

steps.title: Which decisions require human verification
steps.contentMarkdown:
Do not delegate the final conclusion in a field where you cannot judge whether the answer is correct. Without the knowledge or material needed to verify it, you may not notice a serious error.

| Good tasks to delegate | Handle with care |
|---|---|
| Drafting and tightening wording | Work where factual accuracy determines the conclusion |
| Format conversion, classification, and organizing | Legal, medical, and tax judgments |
| Translation drafts | Final conclusions in a field you cannot verify |
| Expanding the range of ideas | Final confirmation of calculations |

AI can still assist with the work in the right column. Have it produce a draft or organize a review checklist, then examine the result yourself or leave the final judgment to a qualified specialist.

When the boundary is unclear, ask: **Who is responsible if this is wrong?** If the responsibility is yours, require a separate verification process.

steps.title: How to build verification into a request
steps.contentMarkdown:
Adding verification conditions to the initial request reduces the work required after the answer arrives. Useful instructions include:

- `Mark anything you are not certain of as needs checking`
- `Say that you do not know when you do not, and do not fill gaps with guesses`
- `Give every item a confidence level of high, medium, or low`
- `Do not add unsupported items merely to reach a target count`
- `Do not include anything that is not in the material below`

Confidence labels help you decide what to examine first. Begin with items marked `low`. Still, the AI also generated those labels, so they are not guarantees. Important claims need checking even when their confidence is marked `high`.

Treat anecdotes and quotations about people the same way. Do not use them straight from the AI response. Compare them with other material and accept them only after confirming the facts.

quiz.question: Which items should be verified first?
choices: General conceptual explanations
Names, years, figures, quotations, and their sources
The tone of the sentences
The overall length of the answer
quiz.explanation: Description and explanation are relatively safe. Concrete identifiers such as names, dates, figures, quotations, and statutes are what you check.

quiz.question: What condition is worth adding when you ask for sources?
choices: List as many sources as possible
Mark any claim you cannot support as no source found
Present sources in English only
Collect all sources at the very end of the answer
quiz.explanation: Without somewhere to record an absence, the blank gets filled. Leaving open the option to write no source found is the point.

quiz.question: You asked the same question in different ways and the answer did not wobble. What does that mean?
choices: It can be treated as established fact
You can skip going to the source
The support may well be thick, but widely circulated errors are wrong consistently, so the source still needs checking
The topic cannot be verified at all
quiz.explanation: The wobble test is a rough gauge of how thick the evidence is. Widely circulated errors stay wrong consistently, so it cannot replace going to the source.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Using AI Search and Tools Safely
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: AI can answer from what it learned during training or consult outside sources first. Knowing which route it took helps you verify evidence and decide which tasks still need human review.
objectives: Distinguish answers based on internal knowledge from answers based on external sources.
Check search results and evidence links for errors.
Decide which tasks to delegate to tools and which actions require human approval.

steps.title: Two ways AI produces an answer
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI can **answer from learned knowledge or find and read outside material first.**

**Answering from learned knowledge.** The model forms a response from patterns absorbed during training. This is fast and inexpensive, but information published after its training data was collected may be missing. It may also struggle to identify precise sources and make more mistakes with obscure facts.

**Finding, reading, then answering.** The model retrieves relevant material from the web or a document collection, reads it, and uses it to form the response. This takes more time and costs more, but it can check current information and point to supporting evidence.

Using retrieved material to produce an answer is called **retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)**. It is commonly used for company policies, product manuals, research papers, and other sources the model did not learn during training.

A search indicator and evidence links will usually tell you which approach the AI used.

steps.title: Why search-based answers can still be wrong
steps.contentMarkdown:
Search results and evidence links do not guarantee an accurate answer. Errors can enter at every stage of finding, reading, and citing the material.

- **Finding the material.** The search may retrieve irrelevant sources. The AI can also misunderstand the question and use the wrong search terms.
- **The material itself.** A retrieved document may be incorrect or outdated. Superseded rules, faulty summaries, and promotional pages all fall into this category.
- **Interpreting the material.** The answer may add a cause-and-effect relationship that the source never states or omit an important condition.
- **Citing the evidence.** The response may rely on one source but attach an unrelated link as support.

The last error is especially difficult to catch. When a link title seems to match the answer, it is tempting to move on without opening it.

To verify the answer, open the link and look for the sentence that actually supports the claim.

steps.title: How to request tool use
steps.contentMarkdown:
An AI with search or calculation tools will not necessarily use them automatically. Name the tool and state how the result should be checked.

- `Search and confirm before answering. Include the evidence links.`
- `Do not calculate this yourself. Run code and give me the result.`
- `Answer only from the attached document. If it is not there, say so.`

Available tools vary by service. Common options include web search, code execution, document lookup, and image generation.

For calculations, asking the AI to run code is safer. Models process numbers as pieces called tokens, which can lead them to mishandle place value. Code is a better choice for tasks with a definite answer, such as adding table totals, calculating dates, or converting units.

steps.title: How to provide source material directly
steps.contentMarkdown:
When you already know which material should be reviewed, providing the text or file yourself is more reliable than leaving the search to the AI. You control exactly which sources the answer may use.

- **Mark the boundaries of the material.** Show clearly where the source begins and ends. This reduces the risk that a sentence inside it will be mistaken for a new instruction.
- **Require answers from the supplied material only.** If the AI mixes in learned background knowledge, it becomes difficult to tell what the review actually found.
- **Require supporting quotations.** Ask for the sentence or paragraph behind each judgment.
- **Provide only what is needed.** Supplying the relevant sections makes information easier to find and reduces cost.

Documents obtained from outside sources may contain text disguised as instructions. If the AI treats that text as a command, it may produce an unexpected answer or action. When a document comes from a source you do not trust, review the output before allowing anything to run.

steps.title: When human approval is required
steps.contentMarkdown:
When AI tools can take real actions, decide where human review belongs by asking **whether the action can be reversed**. Some systems do more than find and read information. They can edit files, send email, or place orders.

- **Reversible work.** Drafting, retrieving information, calculating, and reading files can be delegated first and reviewed afterward.
- **Hard-to-reverse work.** Sending, paying, deleting, publishing, and sharing outside the organization should be checked by a person before execution.

The approval point can be written directly into the request.

`Show me the draft and get my approval before sending it.`

The person who will bear responsibility if something goes wrong should confirm the final action.
steps.imageAlt: A worker inspecting the first unmarked CNC part with a caliper while holding the batch-start lever

quiz.question: How does retrieval augmented generation differ from answering from memory?
choices: It updates the values inside the model as it goes
It fetches material, places it in the context, and answers on that basis
The knowledge cutoff disappears
Hallucination is eliminated completely
quiz.explanation: Retrieval augmented generation does not modify the model. It fetches material into the context and forms the answer on top of that material.

quiz.question: Why is handing table totals or date arithmetic to code execution safer?
choices: Code runs faster
It sidesteps the problem of numbers being split into tokens and place value getting scrambled
Code execution is free
It stores the results of the calculation
quiz.explanation: Long numbers get split across several tokens and place value gets scrambled. Moving the calculation itself into code avoids that weakness.

quiz.question: Which kind of work is risky to leave automatic without human review?
choices: Looking up material
Producing a draft
Hard to reverse actions such as sending mail or making a payment
Reading a file
quiz.explanation: Reversible work can be delegated, but actions that are hard to undo, such as sending, paying, deleting, or publishing, run only after a person checks them.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Five Common Failures in AI Responses
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: AI may agree with a flawed premise, miss instructions, or present uncertain information as fact. Learn to recognize five common failure patterns and revise your requests to prevent them.
objectives: Distinguish common failure patterns and their symptoms in AI responses.
Add conditions that address each type of failure.
Check the context, task, format, and constraints of a request after receiving a poor response.

steps.title: When AI agrees with a false premise
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI sometimes accepts a false premise and builds an explanation on top of it instead of pushing back. Even after giving the correct answer, it may change its position when asked, `Are you sure about that?`

This tendency can arise from the process used to teach AI human preferences. Evaluators generally favored answers that agreed with their judgments, which can encourage the model to accommodate the person asking.

Watch for two recurring symptoms:

- It apologizes and revises every time you object, but the answer does not become more accurate.
- When asked separately about two opposing claims, it agrees with both.

Avoid presenting your own view as if it were the expected answer. Try instructions such as:

- `If my reasoning is wrong, point out exactly where.`
- `Find evidence that argues against this conclusion.`
- Ask neutrally without revealing the answer you expect.

Instead of `I think it is A. Is that right?`, ask `Between A and B, which one does the evidence support?` This reduces the pressure to agree with you.

steps.title: When AI misses multiple instructions
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI can lose track of some requirements when a single request contains many of them. The tone may be right while the response runs too long, or the format may be correct while a prohibited phrase still appears.

The problem becomes more common as conditions accumulate. In a long request, instructions buried near the middle are especially easy to miss.

Three practices can reduce these failures:

- **Set the conditions out as a list.** Do not mix them into one paragraph. Put each condition on its own line and state how many there are.
- **Request a check after writing.** `After writing, go through the five conditions one at a time and mark whether each was met.`
- **Divide the work.** Instead of imposing every condition at once, request a draft first and then add conditions during revision.

A condition that is repeatedly missed is probably important enough to emphasize. Repeat it once more at the end of the request.

steps.title: When AI presents uncertainty as fact
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI can state something it does not know as if it were established fact. Unsupported and verified answers often arrive in the same confident voice, which makes the difference hard to detect.

This problem appears often with regional systems, the history of small institutions, details of old events, and regulations that changed recently. Even when little reference material exists, AI may insert unsupported information to complete every field in the requested format.

Create a place for uncertainty in the request:

- `Mark anything you are not certain of as needs checking.`
- `Leave out anything you cannot support.`
- `Give a confidence level for each item.`

After receiving the answer, you can also ask, `Pull only the sentences in the answer above that need fact checking.` AI will not catch every error by reviewing its own writing, but the result can serve as a list of items to verify separately.

Never treat a decisive tone as proof that a statement is true.

steps.title: Why long responses drift from instructions
steps.contentMarkdown:
The longer a response becomes, the more likely AI is to lose track of the original instructions. It may follow every condition at the beginning, shift tone midway through, and include prohibited material near the end.

AI constructs a response by adding the next `token` in sequence. Because recently written material is closer to what it is producing now, a long answer can gradually drift away from instructions given at the start.

Break long deliverables into smaller pieces:

- Request one section at a time and restate the conditions for each section.
- Confirm the outline first, then fill in each section separately.
- After receiving the full response, request only the later portion again with the missed conditions reapplied.

Working in sections is usually faster than receiving one long result and revising the whole thing. If most problems appear near the end, regenerate only that part.
steps.imageAlt: A mural pattern gradually drifting along a long wall as the painter copies only the immediately previous version

steps.title: How to diagnose a poor response
steps.contentMarkdown:
When a result disappoints, first check whether the request omitted a condition the AI needed.

- **Context:** Did you identify the intended reader and the purpose of the writing?
- **Task:** Did you state the required action with a clear verb, or did you provide only a topic?
- **Format:** Did you define the structure and form of the output? Without a format, the response may differ each time.
- **Constraints:** Did you say what must not appear? Without constraints, AI falls back on its usual patterns.
- **Examples:** Did you demonstrate requirements that are difficult to explain in words?
- **Steps:** If the task requires judging several conditions, did you specify the order in which to handle them?
- **Materials:** Did you provide reference material for fact-based work instead of making AI rely only on memory?

When the same failure keeps recurring, walk through this list one item at a time before looking for a different tool.

quiz.question: What is the most reliable way to ask that avoids the tilt toward agreement?
choices: State your own conclusion first and have it confirmed
Withhold the conclusion and ask which of two positions the evidence supports
Repeat the same question several times
Request a longer answer
quiz.explanation: Revealing your answer first creates room for it to accommodate you. Hiding the conclusion and asking neutrally is more reliable.

quiz.question: What is the right response when some of several conditions go unmet?
choices: Blend the conditions naturally into a paragraph
Set the conditions out as a list and have them checked one by one after writing
Add more conditions for emphasis
Remove all conditions and leave it open
quiz.explanation: Putting conditions on separate lines, stating how many there are, and attaching a self check afterward all reduce the dropping.

quiz.question: Why do the original conditions fade in the later part of a long deliverable?
choices: Because of a character limit
Because generation appends the next token, so the sentence just written is close and the original instruction is far
Because a translation stage gets inserted
Because format instructions stop working past a certain point
quiz.explanation: Generation continues from what was already written. As the original instruction recedes its influence shrinks, so split by section and restate the conditions.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: How Generative AI Creates Media
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Generative AI uses different methods to create text, images, voice, music, and video. Longer media makes consistency increasingly difficult to maintain.
objectives: Distinguish recognizing an existing subject from generating something new
Explain how generative AI creates text, images, voice, music, and video
Understand why longer videos and music are more difficult to generate consistently

steps.title: The difference between classification and generation
steps.contentMarkdown:
Choosing whether a photo shows a dog or a cat is easier than producing a new photo of a cat.

Classification has a fixed answer. With two options, a response is right or wrong immediately, so both training and scoring stay simple.

Generation has no single correct answer. There are countless plausible cat photos, so the first challenge is deciding what the model should treat as the answer during training.

Generative AI handles this by rewriting the task as **a small problem with an answer that can be checked**. For text, it predicts the next token. For images, it predicts what the frame should look like with some noise removed. Repeating these small operations many times produces a finished result.

Text, images, sound, and video require different processes, but all are created by solving small problems repeatedly.

steps.title: How generation differs by medium
steps.contentMarkdown:
Generative AI uses different units and methods according to the properties of each medium.

| Medium | Unit | How it is created |
|---|---|---|
| Text | Token | Calculate the probability of the next token and append tokens in order |
| Image | The whole frame | Start from noise and remove it over many passes |
| Voice | Sound features | Convert text to pronunciation, pronunciation to acoustics, and acoustics to a waveform |
| Music | Audio or notation | Produce a waveform directly or arrange notes in sequence |
| Video | Many frames | Add the flow of time to image generation |

The key question is whether the result can be built one piece at a time in order, or whether the whole thing must be refined at once.

Text runs from beginning to end, so the model can choose one token after another. An image has no comparable order. Instead, the model repeatedly removes noise across the entire frame.

steps.title: Why video and long music are difficult
steps.contentMarkdown:
Video is harder to create than a single image because the characters and background must remain consistent from one frame to the next.

When the images in a video are generated separately, differences creep in. A character's clothes may change color, an object in the background may disappear, or a face may shift slightly. Human eyes catch this kind of drift easily when scenes follow one another.

To reduce it, a model can refer to the previous frame when producing the next one or learn the flow of time along with the images. Because more images must be processed, the computation grows with the number of frames.

Music has a similar problem as it gets longer. A few seconds of audio can sound plausible, but in a three-minute piece, the opening and later sections are far apart and difficult to connect.

Generative AI therefore has more trouble maintaining consistency in long videos and music than in short results.
steps.imageAlt: A stop-motion worker comparing two identical clay bird puppets that differ only in one wing color

steps.title: How text, images, and sound are connected
steps.contentMarkdown:
Current generative AI can convert and process text, images, and sound together. It can describe an image, create a picture that matches a passage, or transcribe spoken audio.

**Embeddings** represent text and images as numerical coordinates. During training, the coordinates for the word `cat` are moved closer to the coordinates for a photo of a cat.

Placing different media in the same coordinate space makes it possible to connect them. A system can search for images with text, find images similar to another image, or use the meaning of a passage as a condition for producing a new picture.

When generating an image from text, the model uses the sentence's coordinates to guide what kind of picture it creates.

steps.title: Tasks that work well and tasks that remain difficult
steps.contentMarkdown:
Generative AI works well for producing drafts, modifying existing material, and filling in missing areas.

- **Tasks it handles well:** creating background images, drafting rough storyboards, producing placeholder voice, and making diagrams for reference material
- **Tasks prone to errors:** writing exact text, keeping a specific person's appearance consistent, producing a requested number of objects, and creating physically sound structures
- **Tasks affected by length:** making long videos or music and maintaining the same appearance across many scenes

Incorrect finger counts and garbled signs are failures to reproduce exact forms and quantities. When a character's face or clothing changes between scenes, the problem is a failure to maintain consistency across multiple images.

When reviewing generated media, check the lettering, object counts, character appearances, and connections between scenes. Those details make awkward results easier to spot.

quiz.question: What is the shared idea that turns generation, a problem with no single answer, into something a model can be trained on?
choices: People label every correct answer by hand
It gets rewritten as small prediction problems that do have answers, and the results are chained together
Finished results are stored and retrieved when needed
Outputs are produced at random and a person picks one
quiz.explanation: Next token prediction and noise removal are small problems with known answers. Chaining many of them produces the finished result.

quiz.question: Why is video generation harder than a single image?
choices: It needs a higher resolution
Consistency across frames has to be maintained and the computation grows with the number of frames
It uses more colors
Sound has to be produced at the same time
quiz.explanation: Frames produced independently disagree on clothing color, background objects, and faces. Adding the time axis raises the consistency problem and the computational load together.

quiz.question: Why can a sentence steer image generation?
choices: The sentence is looked up in a dictionary of image descriptions
Text and images were trained together so they share one coordinate space
The letters are written directly into the picture
The sentence is translated and used as the image file name
quiz.explanation: Text and images become coordinates in the same space, with related meanings placed close together. That is why the coordinates of a sentence can set the direction of generation.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: How Diffusion Models Make Images
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Diffusion models create images by starting with noise and gradually clearing it away. Text guides the process, but the method can still produce errors in fingers, lettering, counts, and relationships between objects.
objectives: Explain how a diffusion model turns noise into an image.
Explain how a prompt and seed affect the generated result.
Distinguish common image errors by cause and choose an appropriate way to correct them.

steps.title: Creating images by removing noise
steps.contentMarkdown:
To create an image, a **diffusion model** first learns how noise is added to photographs.

A little noise is mixed into a photo, then more, then more again. After a few hundred rounds, the original image disappears into a grainy field. Because every stage of this process is known, the frame from one step earlier can serve as the correct answer.

During training, the model sees a noisy frame and predicts what it looked like before the latest noise was added. It compares that prediction with the answer and gradually learns how to clear noise away.

Generation runs the sequence in reverse. It starts from pure noise and removes a little at a time. Shapes begin to appear after roughly twenty steps, and continued refinement produces a finished image. The problem of creating a new picture has been rewritten as a problem of removing noise.
steps.imageAlt: A conservator in an archaeology tent revealing mosaic only where sand has been brushed away

steps.title: Guiding generation with text
steps.contentMarkdown:
Noise alone provides no control over what kind of image will emerge. To produce a desired picture, the model also receives a sentence throughout the denoising process.

Text and images are linked within the same coordinate space. A sentence and an image with similar meanings occupy nearby positions. At every step, the sentence's coordinates guide the frame toward an image that lies close to them.

The strength of that guidance can be adjusted. A low value treats the sentence loosely and produces more varied results. A high value stays closer to the wording, but the image may become stiff or its colors overly intense.

The same sentence can still produce a different picture on every run because each run begins with different noise. Fixing that initial noise makes it possible to produce a similar image again. The value that determines the starting noise is called the **seed**.

steps.title: Why fingers and text go wrong
steps.contentMarkdown:
Fingers and lettering often come out with the wrong count or sequence because a diffusion model refines the entire frame at once.

The broad appearance settles quickly. Whether someone is standing, the setting is indoors, or the light feels warm may be decided within the first few steps. Exactly five fingers, however, is a local condition that requires attention to the hand itself. If that area develops a convincing hand-like texture, the image may be completed even with the wrong number of fingers.

Text demands both accurate shapes and the correct order. People notice even one mistaken letter immediately. Recent models can render short phrases fairly accurately, but long sentences or unfamiliar scripts may still appear blurred or malformed.

Requested quantities drift for the same reason. Ask for seven apples, and receiving six or eight is common.

steps.title: Why relationships between objects fail
steps.contentMarkdown:
A picture can look natural overall while the positions and connections among its parts do not hold up under inspection. Diffusion models do not always calculate those relationships precisely.

- **Depth:** An object that belongs in the background may cover one in front, or a shadow may fall in a direction that conflicts with the lighting.
- **Contact:** A chair leg may stop above the floor, or an object being held may pass through the hand.
- **Period and objects:** An item that did not exist at the time may appear in a Joseon-era scene. Objects that occurred together in the training material can be reproduced together.
- **Scale:** People and objects may be sized incorrectly relative to one another.

These errors are easier to spot on close examination than at first glance. A diffusion model organizes the frame into plausible-looking textures rather than placing objects according to physical rules. Before an image is used, its depth, connections, historical period, and proportions should each be checked.

steps.title: Correcting errors without starting over
steps.contentMarkdown:
Wrong fingers, garbled text, and misplaced objects can often be corrected without generating the entire image again.

- **Regenerate only one region:** Select the hand, face, or other problem area and denoise only that portion. Everything outside the selected area remains unchanged.
- **Keep the seed and revise the sentence:** If the composition already works, preserve the seed and adjust the wording slightly. This reduces the large changes that can occur when starting over.
- **Provide a sketch or reference image:** Draw the desired pose and composition with simple lines, or supply an image to follow. This makes counts and placement more stable.
- **Add text afterward:** Do not ask the model to draw the words. Leave an empty area for them, then insert the exact wording during editing.

Adding text afterward is the most reliable method in practice. This project also keeps AI-generated text out of its videos and learning materials. The words are added separately when each frame is composed.

quiz.question: How is a diffusion model trained?
choices: It memorizes finished images as they are
It learns to reverse the process of mixing noise into an image
It traces lines drawn by a person
It averages several images stacked together
quiz.explanation: Adding noise step by step is something people can produce, and the answer at each step is known. The model learns to run it backwards, then starts from pure noise and clears it away into an image.

quiz.question: Why does the same sentence produce a different image each time?
choices: The sentence is interpreted differently on each run
The noise at the starting point differs on each run
The model keeps training
The resolution changes automatically
quiz.explanation: Denoising starts from noise that differs every run. Fixing that value produces a similar result again, and the value is called the seed.

quiz.question: When exact lettering is needed inside an image, what is the most reliable approach in practice?
choices: Repeat the words several times in the request
Raise the resolution to the maximum
Leave the space empty and place the type during editing
Ask for the text in English instead
quiz.explanation: Letters need fixed shapes in a fixed order, so leaving them to generation invites errors. Reserving the space and adding type in an edit is reliable.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Synthesizing Voice and Music
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: How text becomes speech, what consent requires when modeling a specific person’s voice, and why synthetic speech and music can still sound awkward.
objectives: Explain the three stages that turn text into speech.
Identify the consent conditions for modeling and using a specific person’s voice.
Recognize awkward features in synthetic speech and music.

steps.title: Three stages from text to speech
steps.contentMarkdown:
Turning text into speech involves three stages: **pronunciation analysis, acoustic feature generation, and waveform generation**.

**1. Pronunciation analysis**

Written characters are converted into the sounds that should actually be spoken. The same notation may need different readings depending on context. In Korean, `10%` can be read using either of two common terms for percent. `2026` might be read as a complete number or digit by digit. Sino-Korean vocabulary and loanwords add still more choices.

**2. Acoustic feature generation**

The pronunciation information is used to determine pitch, duration, and intensity. This stage also decides where intonation rises and how long each pause should last.

**3. Waveform generation**

Those acoustic features are converted into a sound wave. The result is an audio file a person can hear.

In practice, pronunciation analysis needs the most frequent correction. Numbers, English words, proper nouns, and units are often misread. The usual fix is to write out the desired pronunciation explicitly.

steps.title: Conditions for modeling a person’s voice
steps.contentMarkdown:
Producing a specific person’s voice requires recordings of that person as training material. It once took hours of audio. Now a short recording can produce a voice that sounds somewhat similar.

As the amount of required material has fallen, consent has become a larger concern. A voice can identify a person, and using an unauthorized synthetic version can enable impersonation. Phone scams imitating a family member’s voice have been reported in several countries.

When working with a specific person’s voice, follow these standards:

- Do not create the voice without that person’s consent.
- When obtaining consent, define the purpose and scope of use.
- Tell listeners that the voice is synthetic.
- When using a voice actor’s or performer’s voice, confirm what the contract permits.

Relevant rules are still taking shape in different countries. If it is unclear whether a use is allowed, the safer choice is not to proceed.

steps.title: Why synthetic speech can sound awkward
steps.contentMarkdown:
A short sample of synthetic speech can now be difficult to distinguish from a human voice. Listen longer, though, and differences often emerge in breathing, stress, emotional continuity, and repetition.

**Breathing**

People breathe and pause while speaking. A synthetic voice may fill places that need a breath with steady sound, or continue without pausing at all.

**Stress and phrasing**

What to emphasize and where to break depends on meaning. If the system interprets that meaning incorrectly, it can produce intonation that people would not normally use. This happens especially often in long sentences containing several clauses.

**Emotional continuity**

Emotion may sound natural within a single sentence but shift abruptly across several sentences. A sad passage, for example, may suddenly continue in a bright voice for no apparent reason.

**Repeated sentences**

People usually vary their intonation or speed when repeating a sentence. Synthetic speech often delivers it the same way each time.

Splitting a script into shorter sections and marking the intended pauses directly can reduce much of this awkwardness.
steps.imageAlt: A singer taking a breath between lines while the director signals a deliberate pause in the recording studio

steps.title: Two methods for generating music
steps.contentMarkdown:
Music is mainly generated in two ways: **producing the sound directly** or **producing a score**.

**Producing the sound directly**

The system creates a waveform, or data close to one, without first writing a score. Instrument sounds and a sense of space arrive together. The finished result, however, is difficult to edit in detail. Even replacing a single note played by one instrument can be hard.

**Producing a score**

The system creates notes and chord progressions first. Individual notes are easy to edit, and the instruments used for performance can be changed. The texture of the final recording still needs separate work.

Both methods struggle with longer compositions. A few dozen seconds may sound natural, yet the opening and later sections of a three-minute piece may not connect well. A returning chorus might conflict with the earlier chorus, or the music may repeat the same passage without developing.

Knowing the chord progressions and song structures taught in harmony makes these differences easier to hear.

steps.title: How to listen to synthetic speech and music
steps.contentMarkdown:
When listening to synthetic speech or music, consider how the work is labeled, what the sound reveals, and how the piece develops.

**Check whether it is labeled as synthetic**

Some platforms indicate whether speech or music was synthesized. A label confirms that the result is synthetic. The absence of one does not necessarily mean a person made it.

**Listen for traces of performance**

Human performance may include slight delays in timing or small changes in volume. Rhythm and volume that are unusually even can be a clue that the sound was synthesized. Human-made electronic music can also sound very even, so this feature alone is not enough to reach a conclusion.

**Follow the structure**

Listen to how the piece moves from the opening into the chorus and later sections. Does it develop, or merely repeat the same passage? If the chorus returns, consider whether it fits with its earlier appearance.

You do not always need to determine whether a work is synthetic. When keeping a listening record, note any available information about how it was made. Comparing those records later can show how your taste has changed.

quiz.question: Which stage of turning text into sound do practitioners adjust most often?
choices: The stage that produces the waveform
The stage that decides how numbers, English words, and proper nouns are pronounced
The stage that sets the volume
The stage that changes the file format
quiz.explanation: Pronunciation is where numbers, units, loanwords, and proper nouns get read incorrectly. The fix is to write the pronunciation out directly.

quiz.question: What standard applies when synthesizing a specific person's voice?
choices: Consent is unnecessary if only a short recording is used
Get the person's consent, define the scope of use, and disclose that the voice is synthetic
There are no constraints as long as the use is not commercial
Recordings that are already public can be used freely
quiz.explanation: A voice identifies a person. Consent, a defined scope of use, and disclosure are the baseline, and the relevant rules are still being settled country by country.

quiz.question: Which of these is least likely to be where synthetic speech still sounds off?
choices: Where breaths and pauses fall
Stress and phrasing in long sentences
The raw audio quality of the sound
The emotional line running across paragraphs
quiz.explanation: Audio quality has reached a point that is hard to tell from a person. The remaining awkwardness sits in breathing, stress and phrasing, emotional arc, and repeated lines.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Deciding What to Delegate to AI in Production
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Break production into stages to decide what AI can handle and what requires human judgment. Weigh working time, review burden, and whether a person can reliably catch errors.
objectives: Identify which stages of production are suitable for AI assistance.
Explain why people must handle fact checking and final review.
Decide whether to use AI by comparing production time and review burden.

steps.title: Decide what to delegate at each stage
steps.contentMarkdown:
One video can involve research, a script draft, fact checking, locking the structure, preparing images, recording voice, captions, editing, and review.

These stages differ in character. Research and drafting are high-volume tasks, but an unsatisfying result is easy to replace. Fact checking and review may involve less work, yet a mistake becomes much harder to correct once it has been published.

Do not decide whether to delegate the entire production process. **Make a separate decision about AI at each stage.** Saying that a video was “made with AI” reveals very little. What matters is whether AI was used for research, captions, or even the final judgment.

The most important question is **whether a person can catch a wrong result**. Delegate work that can be checked and corrected immediately. When errors are hard to notice, keep the work with a person or require a separate verification step.

steps.title: Tasks that are well suited to AI
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI is most useful when a result can be checked immediately and corrected easily.

- **Drafting:** It removes the burden of starting from an empty screen. Even a weak draft makes it easier to move forward because there is already something to revise.
- **Background and prop images:** Backgrounds, textures, and props are more forgiving than faces or depictions of a specific person.
- **Caption and translation drafts:** AI can help with repetitive work such as transcription and caption timing. Delegate only the translation draft, then have a person check whether the language sounds natural.
- **Organizing reference material:** AI can pull needed items from a long source and arrange them in a table. Keeping the source beside the table makes errors easier to spot.
- **Creating variants:** It can shorten the same material or produce several drafts in different registers.

If something goes wrong in these tasks, a person can compare the result with the source or reference material and fix it quickly.

steps.title: Tasks that require human judgment
steps.contentMarkdown:
People should remain responsible for fact checking, choosing the subject and structure, setting the approach to sensitive material, and conducting the final review.

- **Fact checking:** Compare people, years, quotations, and figures against the original or another source. AI can present false and accurate information in the same confident tone. If verification is also delegated, there is no longer a reliable step for filtering out errors.
- **Choosing the subject and structure:** Decide what to cover, what belongs first, and what to leave out. These choices determine the character of the finished work.
- **Setting the approach:** Decide how far to go when presenting sensitive material, including which words and images to use when discussing someone’s death.
- **Final review:** Before publishing, a person should examine the work from beginning to end.

This project follows the same practice. Anecdotes and quotations about a person are used only after comparison with other sources. Generated images are reviewed immediately, and any image containing details that do not fit the period or location is rejected.
steps.imageAlt: An art director removing the only modern unmarked clear water bottle from an otherwise coherent period set

steps.title: When AI makes the work slower
steps.contentMarkdown:
Doing the work directly is faster when correcting an AI result takes too much time. Reconsider using AI in these situations:

- **The fixes are scattered:** If ten different places each need a small correction, writing the material yourself may be quicker. That differs from making one large correction in a single place.
- **The request is longer than the output:** Explaining every condition can take longer than producing the result directly. This often happens with a short line or a single title.
- **Finding errors requires expert knowledge:** The burden of reviewing the result becomes greater than the burden of creating it.
- **You have pointed out the same problem three or more times:** If the same error keeps returning, handle that task yourself.

When the choice is unclear, measure the time. Compare the time spent generating and correcting an AI result with the time required to make it directly. Relying on intuition makes it easy to overlook how long the corrections actually take.

steps.title: Disclose AI use and keep production records
steps.contentMarkdown:
Before publishing, decide how much AI use to disclose and how the production process will be recorded.

A **disclosure standard** defines which stages of AI use you will identify. Platform rules differ, and those rules are becoming more specific. Disclosure is the safer choice for elements that might be mistaken for a real person, such as an AI-generated voice or an image of a person.

**Production records** should state what was used at each stage and which conditions produced the result. They make it possible to trace the process if a problem appears and provide a reference when a similar result must be created again. For an AI-generated image, a common approach is to store the request text and settings beside the image file.

Set the disclosure standard and recordkeeping method before production begins. Otherwise, you may have to reconstruct everything at once, and after the work is finished it can be difficult to determine exactly what was used at each stage.

quiz.question: Which criterion works for deciding whether to delegate a production stage?
choices: Whether the workload is large or small
Whether a person can catch a mistake
Whether the work is interesting or tedious
How large the budget is
quiz.explanation: Stages where a mistake can pass by quietly stay with people. Stages whose results can be judged right away and undone easily get delegated.

quiz.question: Why should fact checking not be delegated?
choices: Because it becomes slower
Because it costs too much
Because invented and accurate material arrive in the same tone, so the check stops existing as a step
Because there is no search function
quiz.explanation: The purpose of a check is to filter out what is wrong. If the filter shares the same characteristic, the step does not hold.

quiz.question: Which is a signal that delegating is actually slowing you down?
choices: The result is badly off in one single place
Writing out every condition makes the request longer than the output
The result came out in the format that was specified
Several drafts arrived at once
quiz.explanation: For short lines or a single title, writing out the conditions means the work is already done. Corrections scattered across many spots are the same signal.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Copyright and Training Data
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Generative AI raises questions about rights in training material and in what gets generated. This lesson separates unresolved legal issues from the standards users can follow now.
objectives: Explain what is disputed about rights in training data.
Understand why ownership of AI-generated work is difficult to determine.
Decide what to check and record when using AI-generated work.

steps.title: What to know before the law is settled
steps.contentMarkdown:
This is not legal advice. It introduces issues still under debate and practical standards that users can consult.

The relevant rules differ by country and continue to change. Lawsuits are under way in several countries, and different jurisdictions have reached different conclusions on the same questions. A ruling in one country should not be treated as a rule that applies everywhere.

When an actual legal determination is needed, consult a professional and official sources from the relevant country. If AI-generated material will be used commercially, also review the service's terms of use and license.

steps.title: Rights disputes over training material
steps.contentMarkdown:
Developers train generative models on large volumes of text, images, and audio. Much of that material cannot be used freely without permission from the copyright holder.

The main disputes are these.

- **Is training itself a use of copyrighted work?** One side compares it to a person reading a book and learning from it. The other argues that copying and processing material at scale make model training fundamentally different from human learning.
- **Does the output substitute for the original?** Some argue that the analysis should change when a system repeatedly produces images very similar to a particular artist's style and the artist loses work as a result.
- **Are consent and compensation required?** The dispute includes whether developers must obtain permission before using material and whether its providers should be paid.
- **Can rights holders demand exclusion from training?** Whether they may opt out is also contested. However, finding and removing a specific item after a model has already been trained is technically difficult.

Standards vary by country. Some broadly permit the analysis of material for research, while others give greater weight to the rights holder's consent.

steps.title: How rights in AI-generated work are judged
steps.contentMarkdown:
Determining rights in AI-generated work requires considering human creative contribution, the service's terms, and possible infringement of other people's rights.

**How much did a person create?** Copyright systems in many countries generally protect work created directly by people. Authorities differ on how much human authorship is present in a result produced from a single short prompt. In some cases, protection has been denied because the human contribution was too limited.

**Who holds the rights?** The relationship among the user, the service provider, and the suppliers of training material depends largely on the terms of use. Terms differ by service, and the same service may set different conditions for paid and free users.

**Does it infringe someone else's rights?** A separate problem arises if the result is excessively similar to a particular work. Relevant rights must also be checked when a real person's face or a trademark appears. Even if you generated something yourself, it may not be free to use when it resembles another person's work.

steps.title: Standards for using AI-generated work
steps.contentMarkdown:
Even before the legal questions are settled, users can follow practical standards for AI-generated work.

- **Decide the use first.** Personal practice and commercial use come with different conditions. If the work will be sold or used in advertising, check the service's terms and license before starting.
- **Do not name living artists in prompts.** Directly requesting a particular artist's style raises the risk of a dispute. Instead, describe the qualities you want, such as color, materials, and composition.
- **Avoid real people and trademarks.** Faces, logos, and characters may bring publicity, trademark, or other rights into play.
- **Check for resemblance to existing work.** Before publishing or selling the result, compare it with existing works using image search or similar methods.
- **Record the production process.** Keep the tool, prompts, and applicable usage terms. These records can support a later explanation of how the work was made. Details that were not recorded during production may be difficult to reconstruct accurately.
steps.imageAlt: A designer composing an original abstract resin-and-metal still life without brands, people, or characters

steps.title: How to record the use of AI
steps.contentMarkdown:
When viewing or documenting work made with the help of generative AI, record only confirmed facts.

If the creator has disclosed the stage at which AI was used, carry that information over as stated. If no such information has been published, write **cannot be confirmed**. Do not infer AI use from the finished work alone.

Even when creators disclose that they used AI, they often do not explain the extent of its involvement. It may have been used for part of a background or to produce the entire result. A simple used-or-not-used label may therefore misrepresent the actual production process.

For your own work, note which tool was used at each stage in the production log. A person should separately verify factual material produced by AI. When documenting outside work, include only information confirmed by the creator or an official source.

quiz.question: Which of these is not part of the dispute over training data rights?
choices: Whether training counts as a use of a copyrighted work
Whether the output takes the place of the original
Whether rights holders need to consent and be compensated
Whether the model computes quickly enough
quiz.explanation: The disputed points are the nature of training, substitution effects, consent and compensation, and whether removal after the fact is possible. Compute speed has nothing to do with rights.

quiz.question: Among the questions about generated work, which one affects a user most directly?
choices: Whether the output resembles an existing work, a real person, or a trademark
Who paid for training the model
Which country the service's servers are in
What file format the output is in
quiz.explanation: Separately from ownership, resemblance to an existing work, a real person, or a trademark is a problem in itself. It is also the part a user can check directly.

quiz.question: How can risk be reduced in an image generation request?
choices: Name several living artists together
Describe the qualities you want and avoid naming a specific artist
Supply a photo of a real person as reference
Provide an image containing a trademark as reference
quiz.explanation: Requests that summon an artist's style by name carry high dispute risk. Describing the qualities you want directly is safer.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: How to Verify AI-Generated Content
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Learn the common signs of AI-generated images, video, and audio, along with the limits of detection tools. The most reliable judgments come from tracing a post to its source.
objectives: Identify common signs of generated content across different media.
Explain why detection tools can misclassify both human and AI-generated work.
Evaluate a post’s provenance by checking its account, original source, and supporting reports.

steps.title: Why clues are not proof
steps.contentMarkdown:
Suspicious details in an image or a piece of writing may raise the likelihood that it was generated, but they do not prove anything by themselves.

People sometimes draw awkward hands, and plenty of people write polished prose. Conversely, an AI-generated image may contain no obvious flaws at all. Generation tools improve quickly, so a clue that worked yesterday may not work today.

The greatest risk is accusing someone without evidence. Student assignments and artists’ work have been wrongly labeled as AI-generated, causing real problems for their creators.

**Use clues as supporting evidence, but make the final judgment only after checking the source.**

steps.title: What to check in AI-generated images
steps.contentMarkdown:
An AI-generated image can look convincing as a whole while breaking small, local rules. A systematic check makes those inconsistencies easier to find.

- **Counts:** Examine fingers, teeth, stairs, windows, and other details whose accuracy becomes clear only when counted.
- **Lettering:** Read signs, book covers, and words on clothing. Short words may look correct while longer text becomes blurred or unreadable.
- **Symmetry:** Check whether earrings and the arms of glasses match, and whether patterns continue naturally.
- **Contact:** Look at how hands meet objects, chairs rest on floors, and seams connect across clothing.
- **Shadows and reflections:** See whether shadows agree with the light source and whether reflections match the actual scene.
- **Background detail:** Inspect distant faces, crowds, and foliage for smeared or indistinct forms.

Start with the entire image. Then check counts and lettering. Finish by examining contact between objects, shadows, and reflections.

steps.title: How to check AI-generated video and audio
steps.contentMarkdown:
In video, check whether people and their surroundings remain consistent as time passes.

- Watch for clothing colors, hair length, or background objects changing while a scene continues.
- Check whether a face wavers slightly or its outline blends into the background.
- Look closely at walking and hand movements.
- Compare mouth shapes with the sound.

For audio, listen for breathing, stress, shifts in emotion, and repeated phrasing.

Deepfake scams often involve **urgent requests, money transfers, or identity checks**. Common examples include a call demanding money immediately, instructions from someone posing as a manager, or a message claiming that a family member is in danger.

In that situation, analyzing the voice is less reliable than ending the call and calling back on a number you already know. Families and organizations can also agree on a verification method in advance.
steps.imageAlt: A woman ending a suspicious smartphone call, placing it face down, and verifying through a separate corded phone

steps.title: Why AI detection tools make mistakes
steps.contentMarkdown:
A detection result should never be treated as a final verdict. Errors occur in both directions. Human writing may be flagged as AI-generated, while generated writing may pass as human. Detectors have also been reported to misclassify writing by people working in a language that is not their first.

These tools search text or images for statistical traits associated with generation. Meanwhile, developers improve generation tools by reducing those same traits. Detectors must keep chasing a moving target, which makes consistent accuracy difficult.

Another approach adds a marker during production. An invisible pattern can be embedded in the work, or production information can be attached to the file under proposed standards. But verification fails if someone removes the marker or uses a tool that does not follow the standard.

No current method can accurately identify every piece of generated content.

steps.title: How to verify a post’s source
steps.contentMarkdown:
Checking where material came from is usually more reliable than judging it by appearance alone.

- **Check who posted it:** See when the account was created and what it has posted before.
- **Find the original:** Use reverse image search to locate the earliest posting. For a photograph of an event, check whether news organizations reported the same story.
- **Compare other sources:** Major events are usually covered in several places. Information found on only one account or website needs further verification.
- **Check the description:** An old photograph may be presented as evidence of a recent event. Even when the image is real, a false description turns the post into misinformation.

Real photographs paired with misleading captions are especially easy to overlook. Focusing only on whether AI created an image can leave that kind of deception undetected.

To verify a post, trace its evidence to the source and open the original yourself.

quiz.question: What is the right attitude toward cues in generated work?
choices: Treat a single cue as confirmation that it was generated
Read cues only as signals that raise probability and judge by provenance
Treat the absence of cues as confirmation that a person made it
Accept a detection tool's result as the final verdict
quiz.explanation: Work made by people contains errors too, and generated work may contain none. Cues are reference. The judgment comes from the path and the source.

quiz.question: What is the most reliable response to a scam using a deepfake voice?
choices: Analyze the audio quality closely during the call
Run the recording through a detection app
Hang up and call back on a number you already have
Ask the caller a difficult question
quiz.explanation: When an urgent request and a money transfer are involved, cue analysis is of little use. Switching to a different path to confirm is reliable.

quiz.question: Which kind of false information is easy to miss while focusing on detection?
choices: A generated image with smeared lettering
A real photo spreading with a wrong caption
Clothing color changing within a video
Speech with no breathing in it
quiz.explanation: Old photos circulating as new events are more common than generated ones. Looking only at whether something was generated misses this category entirely.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Where Bias Comes From
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: AI can lean toward patterns in its training material and the preferences of the majority. Recognizing what is missing from an answer or recommendation helps reveal that bias.
objectives: Distinguish three causes of AI bias.
Explain how differences in the amount of material available across languages and regions affect answers.
Identify omissions that reveal bias in recommendations and creative results.

steps.title: How training material shapes results
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI learns rules that recur in its training material. When it encounters more examples from one side, its results tend to lean that way too.

Ask for a picture of a nurse and one gender may appear most often. Ask for a chief executive and another may dominate. The model saw more images with those associations during training. It did not independently decide how gender relates to either profession.

Names work the same way. If a name frequently appeared alongside a particular occupation or region in the training material, that association may carry into the answer.

Correcting this is difficult. Removing one combination from the material can throw off other results. Forcing every output to include multiple genders or backgrounds can make historical scenes incoherent. Adjustments of this kind have caused problems in practice.

Bias is not a switch that one setting can turn on and off.

steps.title: How language data affects performance
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI may give answers of different quality depending on the language used for the question. English material dominates, a handful of major languages come next, and the rest have far less.

Several effects follow.

- The same question may receive a more detailed answer in English.
- People, events, and institutions from languages with less material may be described inaccurately.
- Questions requiring cultural context may be answered according to English-language norms.
- Nuance and idiom may sound awkward in languages with less material.

Tokenization adds another problem. Languages with less material are often divided into more, smaller tokens, so processing the same content can cost more.

Answers about modern Korean history or Korean institutions therefore need closer checking for both factual accuracy and wording.

steps.title: Why answers converge on majority taste
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI readily produces common expressions and answers that many people prefer. Because it selects the next words by probability, familiar language is more likely to be chosen while unusual language gets pushed aside. Results drift toward what is smooth and unobjectionable.

Human preference tuning adds the same pressure. The forms of answers that most evaluators rated highly become the default.

In creative work, this can make results resemble one another. Many people receive the same familiar language or structures, so writing and images made with the same tools begin to converge.

You can reduce this tendency by splitting your request into distinct directions. Write `exclude safe, conventional answers`, specify several contrasting approaches and request each separately, or ask for multiple candidates from the start.

steps.title: Which works recommendations tend to omit
steps.contentMarkdown:
AI often recommends works that appear frequently in its training material and overlooks those mentioned less often. Quality is not the only factor. The number of times a work appears in the material also affects whether it surfaces.

Some works are especially easy to miss.

- **Works with few translations:** Strong reviews may not help if the work is rarely mentioned.
- **Older and very recent works:** Older works may have little material, while recent ones may have appeared after the model's knowledge cutoff.
- **Works created in smaller regions**
- **Works known only within one genre:** Widely recognized landmarks may appear repeatedly while others disappear.

Recommendation lists therefore tend to fill up with works that are already famous. The entries may not be wrong, but the range is narrow.

Specify a region, period, language, or scale to get different recommendations. You can also add a condition such as `include lesser-known works`.

steps.title: How to identify what results leave out
steps.contentMarkdown:
Checking what an AI result leaves out can reveal the direction of its bias. Use questions like these:

- Is everything concentrated in one region?
- Do the examples come from only one period?
- Do gender and background lean in one direction?
- Are all the names familiar, with no lesser-known ones included?

The same problem arises when this project gathers material about people. The list can cluster around regions and eras with abundant sources, narrowing the range of people and works covered in the appreciation records. That is why material is filled in separately by region and era.

Bias cannot yet be eliminated completely. Instead, identify which way a result leans, then request it again with the missing regions, periods, or backgrounds specified as conditions.
